1.1: To you, brethren, other things must be spoken than to those who are of the world, or at least in another way. For it is to them that he gives milk to drink and not meat (1 Cor. 3:2), who keeps the Apostle's pattern in teaching. For that more solid food is to be set before the spiritual, he himself likewise teaches by his own example, saying: 'We speak, not in the words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual'; and again: 'We speak wisdom among the perfect' (1 Cor. 2:13, 6) — such as I indeed trust that you are; unless perhaps it is in vain that you have already for a long time been occupied with heavenly studies, trained in your senses, and meditating on the law of God day and night. Prepare, then, your throats, not for milk, but for bread. There is a bread at Solomon's, and one exceedingly splendid and savory; I mean the book which is inscribed 'The Song of Songs': let it be brought forth, if it pleases, and broken.
1.2: For concerning the words of Ecclesiastes you have been sufficiently instructed, if I am not mistaken, by the grace of God, to recognize and to despise the vanity of this world. And what of the Proverbs? Are not your life and your conduct sufficiently corrected and informed according to the teaching which is found in them? Wherefore, having first tasted those two, which you have nonetheless received as lent from the store of a friend, draw near also to this third bread, that you may perhaps prove what is better. For since there are two evils which alone, or above all, war against the soul — namely, the vain love of the world and the excessive love of self — those two books are known to meet both plagues: the one, with the spade of discipline, pruning everything crooked in conduct and everything superfluous in the flesh; the other, with the light of reason, shrewdly detecting in all the world's glory the paint of vanity, and truly distinguishing it from the solid truth. Finally, to all human studies and worldly desires he preferred to fear God and to keep His commandments. And rightly so. For of true wisdom the former is the beginning, and the latter the consummation: provided it is clear to you that true and consummate wisdom is nothing other than to turn aside from evil and to do good; and likewise that no one can perfectly withdraw from evil without the fear of God, nor is any good work at all [such] apart from the keeping of His commandments.
1.3: The two evils having therefore been driven away by the reading of the two books, one now duly approaches this sacred and contemplative sermon: which, since it is the fruit of both, is altogether to be entrusted only to sober minds and ears. Otherwise, before the flesh has been tamed and given over to the spirit by the pursuits of discipline, before the pomp and burden of the world has been spurned and cast off, the holy reading is unworthily taken up by the impure. For just as the light is poured in vain around blind or closed eyes, so the natural man does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14). Truly, the holy Spirit of discipline will flee the feigned [heart] (Wis. 1:5), that is, an incontinent life; but He will never have a part with the vanity of the world, since He is the Spirit of truth (John 14:17). For what fellowship [is there] between the wisdom that is from above and the wisdom of the world, which is folly before God (1 Cor. 3:19), or the wisdom of the flesh, which is itself an enemy of God? (Rom. 8:7.) But I think that he who comes to us from the road, the friend, will no longer have wherewith to murmur against us, when he too will have taken of this third bread.
1.4: But who shall break it? The head of the house is here; recognize the Lord in the breaking of the bread. For who else is fit? As for me, I would not rashly arrogate that to myself. So look to me, that you look for nothing from me. For I too am one of those who wait, begging along with you the food of my soul, the nourishment of the spirit. Truly, poor and needy, I knock at him who opens and no one shuts, upon the most profound mystery of this sermon. The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord. The little ones have asked for bread; there is no one to break it for them; that is hoped for from your kindness. O most merciful one, break your bread for the hungry — by my hands indeed, if you deign, but by your strength.
1.5: Tell us, I ask, by whom, concerning whom, and to whom it is said, 'Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth', or what sort of beginning is this, so sudden, and made all at once out of the middle of the discourse. For so it breaks into words, as though it had put before us some speaking person, to whom it then introduces this character as answering in turn, whoever she is who demands the kiss. Then, if she either asks or commands that she be kissed by someone or other, why expressly and particularly with the mouth — and his own mouth — as though those who kiss were accustomed to present anything other than the mouth, or a foreign one, and not rather their own? And yet not even this does she say, 'Let him kiss me with his mouth'; but something indeed more unusual: 'With the kiss of his mouth,' she says. And indeed it is a pleasant utterance, which takes its beginning from a kiss, and that certain winning face of Scripture easily affects and allures one to read it, so that what lies hidden in it delights us even to investigate with labor, nor does the difficulty of inquiring perhaps weary us, where the sweetness of the discourse soothes. But whom would such a beginning — a beginning without a beginning — and the novelty of the expression in an old book, not render most attentive? Whence it is clear that this work was composed so not by human talent but by the art of the Spirit, that although it is difficult to understand, it is yet delightful to search out.
1.6: But what — are we to pass over the title? We must not, not even one iota (Matt. 5:18), since we are bidden to gather even the crumbs of the fragments, lest they perish (John 6:12). The title is such: 'Here begin the Songs of Songs of Solomon.' Observe first that the name of the Peaceful One, which is Solomon, suits the beginning of the book, which begins with a sign of peace, that is, with a kiss; and at the same time note that by such beginnings only peaceful minds are invited to understand this scripture — those which can already free themselves from the disturbances of vices and the tumults of cares.
1.7: Further, do not think this also is without purpose, that the inscription is not simply 'Songs' but 'Song of Songs.' For I have read many songs in the Scriptures, and I do not remember any of them to be called so. Israel sang a song to the Lord, because it escaped the sword and yoke of Pharaoh alike, wonderfully delivered and at the same time avenged by the twofold favor of the sea. Yet what it sang was not called the Song of Songs; but, if I remember rightly, the Scripture says: 'Israel sang this song to the Lord' (Exod. 15:1). Deborah, too, sang (Judg. 5:1), Judith also sang (Jth. 16:1), and the mother of Samuel sang (1 Sam. 2:1); some of the prophets also sang, and none of them is read to have called his song the Song of Songs. Indeed, if I am not mistaken, you will find that all of them sang for some advantage received by themselves or theirs: for example, for the gaining of a victory, for the escape from peril, or for the obtaining of whatever benefit of a thing they had longed for. So then many sang, each for his own reasons, lest they be found ungrateful for divine benefits, according to that saying: 'He will praise you, when you have dealt kindly with him' (Ps. 49:18). But this King Solomon — of singular wisdom, lofty glory, abounding in wealth, secure in peace — is known to have lacked none of those things for the receiving of which he might have wished to sing these. Nor does Scripture itself anywhere seem to signify any such thing.
1.8: Inspired, therefore, by God, he sang the praises of Christ and the Church, the grace of holy love, and the mysteries of the eternal marriage; and at the same time expressed the longing of the holy soul, and composed the song of the epithalamium, rejoicing in spirit, in a pleasant eulogy — yet a figurative one. Doubtless he too veiled his face after the manner of Moses (Exod. 3:6), shining perhaps in this part no less, because in that time as yet no one, or few, were able to behold that glory with unveiled face. Therefore, by reason of its excellence, I judge this nuptial song to have been marked with a title of this kind, that it might deservedly be called, in a special way, the Song of Songs; just as he also to whom it is sung is called in a special way: King of kings and Lord of lords (1 Tim. 6:15).
1.9: Moreover, if you attend to your own experience, have not you also, in the victory by which your faith conquered the world, and at your coming forth from the pit of misery and from the mire of filth, sung a new song to the Lord himself, because he has done wonderful things? Again, when he first set your feet upon the rock and ordered your steps, I think that then too, for the granted newness of life, a new song was put into your mouth — a song to our God. When, upon your repenting, he not only forgave your sins but even promised rewards, did you not, rejoicing in hope much more for the good things to come, sing in the ways of the Lord, because great is the glory of the Lord? But if at some time something closed or obscure in the Scriptures has dawned upon any of you, then indeed it is necessary that, for the nourishment of the heavenly bread received, the sound of one feasting delight the divine ears in the voice of exultation and of confession. But also in the daily exercises and battles, which at no hour are lacking to those who live piously in Christ — from the flesh, the world, the devil — since you experience incessantly in yourselves that the life of man on earth is a warfare (Job 7:1), it is necessary that daily songs be renewed for the victories gained. As often as a temptation is overcome, or a vice subdued, or an imminent peril turned aside, or a snare of the one lying in wait is detected, or some long-standing and inveterate passion of the soul is healed once and for all, or a virtue long and much desired and often asked for is at length obtained by God's gift — what else but, so many times, according to the prophet, does thanksgiving and the voice of praise resound (Isa. 51:3), and for each single benefit God is blessed in his gifts? Otherwise he will be counted ungrateful, when the inquiry comes, who will not be able to say to God: 'Your justifications were to me songs in the place of my pilgrimage' (Ps. 119:54).
1.10: I think you already recognize in yourselves those which in the Psalter are called not 'Songs of Songs' but the 'Songs of Ascents,' because to each of your advances, according to the ascents which each one has set in his heart, a song is to be brought forth to the praise and glory of the one who brings you on. I do not see how otherwise that little verse could be fulfilled — 'The voice of rejoicing and of salvation is in the tents of the righteous' (Ps. 118:15) — or certainly that most beautiful and most salutary exhortation of the Apostle: 'Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord, in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs' (Eph. 5:19).
1.11: But there is a song which by its singular dignity and sweetness rightly surpasses all that we have mentioned, and whatever others there may be; and rightly I would call this the Song of Songs, because it is itself the fruit of all the rest. A song of this kind only the anointing teaches, only experience learns. Let those who have experience recognize it, let the inexperienced burn with desire, not so much of knowing as of experiencing. For it is not a noise of the mouth but a jubilation of the heart; not a sound of the lips but a motion of joys; a consonance of wills, not of voices. It is not heard outside, nor does it resound in public: only she who sings hears it, and he to whom it is sung — that is, the bride and the bridegroom. For it is a nuptial song, expressing the chaste and pleasant embraces of souls, the concord of manners, and the harmonious charity of affections toward one another.
1.12: For the rest, that song is not to be sung or heard by a soul as yet childish and a neophyte, and newly converted from the world, but by a mind already advanced and learned, which by its own advances, God being the guide, has already grown so far as to reach, in a manner, a perfect age and marriageable years. Years, I say, of merits, not of time; made fit for the nuptials of the heavenly bridegroom, such as at length in its place will be more fully described. But the hour is passing, which urges us to go out to the works of our hands — both the poverty and the rule of our order. Tomorrow, in the name of the Lord, we shall follow what we had begun concerning the kiss, because today's sermon has delivered us from the title.

2.1: Often considering the ardor of the desire of the Fathers sighing for the presence of Christ in the flesh, I am pricked with compunction and confounded within myself; and now I scarcely hold back my tears, so ashamed am I of the lukewarmness and the torpor of these miserable times. For to which of us does the bestowal of this grace bring so much joy as the promise had kindled desire in the saints of old? For behold how many will rejoice in this Nativity of his, which is soon to be celebrated! but would that it were over the nativity, and not over vanity! Their burning desire, then, and the affection of devout expectation, that voice breathes to me: 'Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth' (Song 1:1). Whoever then was able to be spiritual had surely felt in the spirit how great a grace would be poured forth upon those lips. Therefore, speaking in the desire of the soul, he kept saying, 'Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth'; surely longing in every way not to be defrauded of a share in so great a sweetness.
2.2: For each one who was perfect was saying: 'Of what use to me are these half-word mouths of the prophets?' Rather let him who is fair in form above the sons of men, let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. I no longer listen to Moses: for he has become to me a man of a more impeded tongue (Exod. 4:10). The lips of Isaiah are unclean (Isa. 6:5): Jeremiah does not know how to speak, because he is a child (Jer. 1:6): and all the prophets are without a tongue. Let him, he of whom they speak, himself speak: let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. Let him no longer speak to me in them, or through them, since the water in the clouds of the air is dark: but let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, whose gracious presence, and the streams of his wonderful teaching, may become in me a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. He whom the Father has anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. 45:7), is not a more abundant grace poured into me from him? if only he deign to kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. His word, surely, living and effectual, is a kiss to me, not indeed a joining of lips, which sometimes feigns a peace of minds; but plainly an infusion of joys, a revelation of secrets, a wonderful and in some manner undivided commingling of the light from above and the enlightened mind. For he who cleaves to God is one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17). Rightly, then, do I not receive visions and dreams, I refuse figures and riddles; even the very appearances of angels I disdain. For my Jesus far surpasses even them by his form and by his beauty. I ask, therefore, not that another, whether angel or man, but that he himself kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. Nor indeed do I presume that I am to be kissed by his very mouth (for this belongs to the unique happiness and the singular prerogative of the man he assumed); but more humbly I ask to be kissed by the kiss of his mouth, which is surely common to the many who can say, 'And of his fullness we have all received' (John 1:16).
2.3: Give heed. Let the mouth that kisses be the Word that assumes; that which is kissed, the flesh which is assumed: but the kiss, which is formed alike by the one kissing and the one kissed, the very person compacted of both, that is, the mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus. For this reason, then, none of the saints presumed to say, 'Let him kiss me with his mouth'; but only, 'With the kiss of his mouth': reserving that prerogative, of course, for him upon whom the mouth of the Word was impressed once and in a singular way, when the fullness of the whole divinity bestowed itself upon him bodily. A happy kiss, and wonderful in its astonishing condescension, in which a mouth is not pressed upon a mouth, but God is united to man. And there, indeed, the contact of lips signifies the embrace of souls: but here the confederation of natures joins things human to things divine, making peace between those which are on earth and those which are in heaven. For he himself is our peace, who has made both one (Eph. 2:14). It was for this kiss, then, that every saint of ancient time was sighing; because they foresaw that gladness and exultation were being stored up upon him, and all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in him (Col. 2:3), and they desired themselves also to receive of his fullness.
2.4: I perceive that what is said pleases you: but take also another sense. It did not lie hidden from the saints, even before the coming of the Savior, that God was thinking thoughts of peace toward the race of mortals (Jer. 29:11). For he would not do a word upon the earth which he did not reveal to his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). Yet this word was hidden from many (Luke 18:34). For in that time faith was rare upon the earth, and hope exceedingly slight even in many of those who were awaiting the redemption of Israel. But they who knew beforehand, they also foretold that Christ would come in the flesh, and peace with him. Whence one of them: 'And there shall be peace,' he says, 'in our land when he comes' (Mic. 5:5). Nay rather, they proclaimed with all confidence, as they had received from God, that through him men would recover the grace of God. Which John, the forerunner of the Lord, also recognized in his own time as fulfilled, and bore witness: 'Grace and truth,' he says, 'came through Jesus Christ' (John 1:17): and so every Christian people now experiences that it is true.
2.5: But while they were foretelling peace, and the author of peace was delaying, the faith of the people was wavering, since there was none to redeem, nor any to save. And so men complained of the delays, that the prince of peace, so often announced, had not yet come, as he had spoken through the mouth of his holy prophets who are from of old: and, holding the promises suspect, they demanded the sign of the promised reconciliation, which is the kiss; as if any one of the people were answering the messengers of peace, 'How long do you hold our souls in suspense?' Already long ago you foretell peace, and it does not come; you promise good things, and still there is turmoil. Behold, this very thing, in many ways and in many manners, both the angels to the fathers, and our fathers, have announced to us, saying: 'Peace, peace; and there is no peace' (Jer. 6:14). If God wishes me to be persuaded of that which, concerning the good pleasure of his will, he already answers by so frequent an embassy, and yet does not show it; let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, and so, in the sign of peace, make me secure concerning peace. For how shall I now believe words? There is rather need that words be confirmed by the work. Let God prove his messengers truthful (if indeed they are his messengers), and let him himself follow them, as they have often promised, because without him they can do nothing. He sent the boy, he took the staff, and as yet there is neither voice nor life (2 Kgs. 4:29-31). I do not rise, I am not raised up, I am not shaken out of the dust, I do not breathe again into hope, unless the prophet himself come down and kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.
2.6: To this is added, that he who professes himself our mediator with God is the Son of God, and is God (1 Tim. 2:5). And what is man, that he should be made known to him, or the son of man, that he should take account of him? What confidence have I, that I should dare to entrust myself to so great a majesty? Whence, I say, do I, earth and ashes, presume that God has a care for me? Besides, he loves his Father, but of me he has no need, nor does he want my goods. How, then, shall it be established for me that my mediator is in no way partial? Yet if truly, as you say, God has determined to have mercy, and is thinking to be still more favorably inclined; let him establish a covenant of peace, and strike a perpetual treaty with me in the kiss of his mouth. That he may not make void the things which proceed from his lips; let him empty himself, let him humble himself, let him bow himself down, and let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. That the mediator, fitting the parties equally, may be suspect to neither, let God the Son of God become man, become the son of man, and make me certain in this kiss of his mouth. Without fear I receive as mediator the Son of God, whom I acknowledge as mine also. He will now plainly be in no way suspect to me: for he is my brother and my flesh. For I think he will no longer be able to scorn me, bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.
2.7: So, then, the ancient complaint was demanding the most holy kiss, that is, the mystery of the Word who was to become incarnate, while faith, wearied by a long and grievous waiting, was failing, and an unbelieving people, overcome by weariness, was murmuring against the promises of God. It is my own devising, if you do not likewise recognize this same thing from the Scriptures. Hence, surely, came those complaining voices, full of murmuring: 'Command, command again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there' (Isa. 28:10). Hence those anxious prayers, full of piety: 'Give a reward, Lord, to those who wait for you, that your prophets may be found faithful.' Likewise: 'Stir up, Lord, the entreaties which the former prophets spoke in your name' (Sir. 36:18, 17). Hence those gentle promises, full of consolation: 'Behold, the Lord will appear, and will not lie: if he delays, wait for him; for coming he will come, and will not tarry' (Hab. 2:3). Likewise: 'His time is near to come, and his days shall not be prolonged' (Isa. 14:1). And in the person of the one promised: 'Behold, I,' he says, 'turn aside to you as a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations' (Isa. 66:12). In these words there plainly appears both the urgency of the preachers and the distrust of the peoples. So, then, the common people were murmuring, and faith was wavering; and, according to the prophecy of Isaiah: 'The angels of peace wept bitterly' (Isa. 33:7). Lest, therefore, the whole human race, while Christ delayed, should perish of despair, weak mortality suspecting that it was despised, and distrusting the grace, so often promised again, of its reconciliation with God; the saints who were certain concerning the Spirit were longing for certainty from the presence of the flesh, and with all urgency were demanding a sign of the peace to be restored, for the sake of the fainthearted and the unbelieving.
2.8: O root of Jesse, who stand as a sign for the peoples! (Isa. 11:10.) How many kings and prophets longed to see you, and did not see! Happy nonetheless above them all is Simeon, whose old age is in abundant mercy! He indeed exulted to see the sign of his desire: and he saw, and rejoiced; and, having received the kiss of peace, he is dismissed in peace, yet not before openly declaring that Jesus was born for a sign that would be spoken against (Luke 2:25-35). It was altogether so. The sign of peace, once it had arisen, was spoken against, but by those who hated peace: for there is peace for men of good will, but for the ill-willed a rock of scandal and a stone of stumbling (Luke 2:14). Herod, finally, was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him (Matt. 2:3): for he came to his own, and his own did not receive him (John 1:11). Happy those shepherds in their night watch, who were counted worthy to see this sign. Already then he was hiding himself from the wise and the prudent, and revealing himself to little ones. And Herod wished to see; but because it was not with a good will, he did not merit it, for it was a sign of peace, given only to men of good will; but to Herod and those like him nothing will be given but the sign of Jonah the prophet. But to the shepherds: 'And this,' says the angel, 'is a sign for you'; for you who are humble, for you who are obedient, for you who are not minded to high things, for you who keep watch and meditate on the law of God day and night: 'This,' he says, 'is a sign for you.' What? What the angels were promising, what the peoples were demanding, what the prophets had foretold, this the Lord has now done, and he shows it to you, that in it the unbelieving may receive faith, the fainthearted hope, the perfect security. This, then, is a sign for you. A sign of what? Of pardon, of grace, of peace, and of a peace that shall have no end. This, then, is the sign: 'You will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes, and laid in a manger' (Luke 2:12). God is nonetheless in him, reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19). He will die for your sins, and will rise again for your justification, so that, justified by faith, you may have peace with God (Rom. 4:25; 5:1). This sign of peace a prophet once proposed that King Ahaz ask of the Lord his God, whether in the height above or in the depth below. But the impious king refused (Isa. 7:11, 12), the wretch not believing that in this sign the lowest things were to be joined to the highest in peace: so that those below also, the Lord descending unto salvation, may themselves receive the sign of peace in the holy kiss; and the spirits above may no less share in the same, when he has returned to the heavens, with eternal sweetness.
2.9: The sermon must be brought to an end: but so that I may gather into a brief summary what has been discussed in it, it is plain that this holy kiss was of necessity granted to the world for two reasons, both that it might produce faith in the weak, and that it might satisfy the desire of the perfect: and further, that the kiss itself is nothing other than the mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, through all ages of ages, Amen.

3.1: Today we read in the book of experience. Turn back to yourselves, and let each one attend to his own conscience upon the things that are to be said. I would find out whether it has ever been granted to any of you to say from the heart: 'Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth' (Song 1:1). For it is not for every man to say this from affection; but if anyone has even once received a spiritual kiss from the mouth of Christ, his own experience surely stirs him, and he gladly seeks it again. I judge that no one can even know what it is, except the one who receives it: for it is hidden manna; and he alone who eats still hungers. It is a sealed fountain, to which a stranger has no access; but he alone who drinks still thirsts. Hear one who has experience of it, how he asks it back. 'Restore to me,' he says, 'the joy of your salvation' (Ps. 51:12). Let not a soul like mine, then, by any means claim this for itself, a soul burdened with sins, still subject to the passions of its own flesh, which has not yet felt the sweetness of the spirit, and is wholly ignorant and untried in inward joys.
3.2: Yet I show a soul that is of this sort a place in the Savior that befits her. Let her not rashly rise to the mouth of the most serene Bridegroom, but let her lie fearful with me at the feet of the most severe Lord, and with the publican, trembling, look upon the earth, not upon heaven (Luke 18:13), lest a face accustomed to darkness, confounded among the lights of heaven, be overwhelmed by the glory, and, struck back by the unaccustomed splendors of the majesty, be wrapped again in the blindness of a thicker dark. Not to you, O soul, whoever you are that are such, not to you let that place seem vile or despicable, where the holy sinner laid down her sins and put on holiness. There the Ethiopian woman changed her skin and, restored to a new brightness, even then answered confidently and truly those who reproached her with the saying: 'I am black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem' (Song 1:4). Do you wonder by what art she could do this, or by what merits she obtained it? Take it in a few words. She wept bitterly, and drawing long sighs from her inmost bowels, shaken within by saving sobs, she vomited out the bitter humors. The heavenly physician came most swiftly to her aid: for his word runs swiftly (Ps. 147:15). Is not the word of God a draught? It is indeed, both strong and vehement, and searching the hearts and reins (Ps. 7:9). For the word of God is living and effectual, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of the joints also and the marrow, and a discerner of thoughts (Heb. 4:12). After the example, then, of this blessed penitent, cast yourself down, you also, O wretched one, that you may cease to be wretched; cast yourself down, you also, upon the earth; embrace the feet, appease them with kisses, water them with tears, with which, however, you wash not him but yourself, and become for him one of the flock of shorn ewes that come up from the washing (Song 4:2); so indeed do not dare to lift your face, suffused with shame and sorrow, until you yourself also hear: 'Your sins are forgiven you' (Luke 7:37-48); until you hear: 'Arise, arise, captive daughter of Zion; arise, shake yourself from the dust' (Isa. 52:1, 2).
3.3: When, then, you have taken the first kiss at the feet, not even so will you presume to rise at once to the kiss of the mouth, but there will be for you, as a step toward it, a certain other kiss between, which you will receive in the second place at the hand: of which take also this account. If Jesus says to me, 'Your sins are forgiven you'; unless I cease from sinning, what will it profit? I have put off my tunic; if I put it on again, how far have I advanced? If I again soil my feet, which I had washed, will the washing have been of any avail? Filthy with every kind of vice, I lay a long time in the mire of the filth; but it will doubtless be worse for one who falls back than for one who lies there. For I remember that he who made me whole said to me: 'Behold, you have been made whole, go, sin no more henceforth, lest something worse happen to you' (John 5:14). But he who gave the will to repent must also add the strength to refrain; lest I repeat the things that must be repented, and make my last state worse than the former. For woe to me, even while I repent, if he at once withdraws the hand, without whom I can do nothing. Nothing, I say, for I can neither repent nor refrain. I hear, accordingly, what the Wise Man counsels: 'Do not,' he says, 'repeat a word in your prayer' (Sir. 7:15). I fear also what the judge threatens against the tree that does not bear good fruit (Matt. 3:10). I confess that for such reasons I am not altogether content with the former grace, by which I am already repentant of my evils, unless I also receive a second, namely that I may bring forth fruits worthy of repentance; and that from then on I may not return to the vomit.
3.4: This, then, remains for me to ask and to receive first, before I presume to touch things higher and more sacred. I do not wish to be made highest all at once; I wish to advance little by little. As much as the shamelessness of a sinner displeases God, so much does the modesty of a penitent please him. You appease him more quickly if you keep to your own measure, and do not seek things higher than yourself. The leap from the foot to the mouth is long and steep, nor is the approach even a fitting one. What then? still freshly sprinkled with dust, will you touch the sacred mouth? yesterday drawn from the mire, are you today presented to the face of glory? Let the passage be for you by the hand. Let that first wipe you, let that raise you up? How does it raise you? By giving that from which you may take confidence. What is that? The beauty of continence, and worthy fruits of repentance, which are the works of piety. These will raise you from the dunghill to the hope of daring things greater. In receiving the gift, then, kiss the hand: that is, give the glory not to yourself, but to his name. Give it once, and give it again, both for the offenses forgiven and for the virtues conferred. Or at least see with what you may fortify your brow against these blows: 'What do you have that you did not receive?' But if you did receive it, why do you glory as if you had not received it? (1 Cor. 4:7.)
3.5: At length, now, having in the two kisses a twofold experience of the divine condescension, perhaps you will not be put to shame in presuming things more holy. For as much as you grow in grace, so much also are you enlarged in confidence. Hence it comes about that you both love more ardently, and knock more confidently, for that which you feel to be lacking to you. And to him who knocks it will be opened. Now that highest kiss, whatever it is of highest condescension and of wonderful sweetness, will not, I believe, be denied to one so disposed. This is the way, this the order. First we fall at the feet, and before the Lord who made us we bewail the things which we ourselves have done. Second, we seek the hand of him who lifts us up and strengthens the feeble knees. At last, when by many prayers and tears we obtain these things, then at last we dare perhaps to lift the head to the very mouth of glory, not only, I say it fearing and trembling, to gaze upon it, but also to kiss it; because the Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord, to whom by clinging in a holy kiss we are made one spirit, by his condescension.
3.6: To you, Lord Jesus, to you has my heart rightly said: 'My face has sought you; your face, Lord, I will seek.' For in the morning you made your mercy heard by me, when, as I first lay in the dust and kissed your revered footprints, you forgave me that I had lived badly. Then, as the day advanced, you gladdened the soul of your servant, when afterward, in the kiss of the hand, you also bestowed the grace of living well. And now what remains, O good Lord, except that now, in the fullness of light and in the fervor of the spirit, graciously admitting me also to the kiss of the mouth, you fill me with joy with your countenance? Show me, O sweetest, O most serene, show me where you pasture, where you lie down at midday. Brethren, it is good for us to be here; but behold, the evil of the day calls us away. For these men, who are just now announced to have come, compel us to break off the sermon, welcome as it is, rather than to finish it. I will go out to the guests, lest anything be wanting to the offices of that charity of which we speak, lest perhaps it happen that it be heard of us also: 'For they say, and do not' (Matt. 23:3). Do you meanwhile pray that God may make the free-will offerings of my mouth pleasing, unto the edification of you yourselves, and unto the praise and glory of his name.

4.1: Yesterday's sermon embraced a certain threefold progress of the soul under the name of three kisses. Has it slipped from you? This I shall have to follow up in today's discussion, according as God shall deign to prepare it, in his sweetness, for the poor. We said, if you recall, that those kisses are taken at the feet, at the hand, and at the mouth, referring each to each. In the first, indeed, the beginnings of our conversion are consecrated; but the second is granted to those who are advancing: the third, further, only perfection experiences, and a rare perfection. From this alone, which has been placed last, this Scripture which we have undertaken to treat took its beginning, and for its sake the remaining two were added by us. Whether of necessity, you yourselves will judge. For I think the very face of the discourse easily admonishes us to require these also. It would be strange indeed if you too do not notice that there really must be another kiss, or other kisses, from which he who said, 'Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,' wished to distinguish that one of the mouth (Song 1:1). For why, when it could have sufficed to say simply, 'let him kiss me,' did he nevertheless, beyond the custom and usage of speaking, add distinctly and expressly, 'with the kiss of his mouth,' unless to show that the very kiss he was asking is the highest, not the only one? Do we not, after all, speak to one another thus: 'Kiss me'; or: 'Give me a kiss': and no one goes on to say, 'With your mouth,' or, 'With the kiss of your mouth'? What? when we are preparing to kiss one another, do we turn our mouths toward one another, which nevertheless we do not require of one another by name? Finally, he who tells, for example, that the traitor was received by the Lord with a kiss, says: 'And he kissed him' (Mark 14:45); nor did he add: 'With his mouth,' or, 'With the kiss of his mouth.' So, surely, has everyone been accustomed to do, both he who writes and he who speaks. These, then, are three affections of souls, or progresses, known and manifest enough at least to those who have experience, when they obtain to look upon either pardon for evils that have been done, or grace for goods that are to be done, or even the presence of him who pardons them and does them good, in that manner indeed in which it is possible in a fragile body.
4.2: For the rest, take more plainly the reason for which I have named the first and the second kisses. A kiss, we all know, is a sign of peace. But if, as Scripture says, our sins separate between us and God (Isa. 59:2), let that which stands between be taken out of the way, and there is peace. When, therefore, we make satisfaction, so that, the sin which separates having been removed, we may be reconciled, what should I call the pardon which we receive but a certain kiss of peace? And that, for the time being, is to be taken nowhere but at the feet. For the satisfaction by which a proud transgression is amended ought to be humble and modest.
4.3: But when, for living more correctly and conducting ourselves more worthily of God, we are also given a certain pleasing familiarity of a fuller grace, we now lift the head from the dust with fuller confidence, about to kiss, as is usual, the hand of the giver; if, however, for the gift received we seek not our own glory but the author's, and ascribe his gifts to him and not to ourselves. Otherwise, if you glory in yourself and not rather in the Lord, you are surely convicted of kissing your own hand and not the Lord's: which, according to the opinion of blessed Job, is the greatest iniquity, and a denial against God (Job 31:28). If, then, according to the testimony of Scripture, to seek one's own glory is to kiss one's own hand, surely he who gives the glory to God is not unfittingly said to kiss the hand of God. And among men, indeed, we see that it is so: servants, namely, of masters whom they have offended are wont to kiss their feet when they ask pardon of them; and the poor the hands of the rich, when they receive a gift from them.
4.4: But because God is spirit (John 4:24), and that simple substance is marked off by no bodily members, there will perhaps be someone who in no way accepts any such thing of him, but demands that the hands or feet of God be shown him by me, and that what I define concerning the kiss of the feet or of the hand be thus proved. But what if I in turn ask of this questioner of mine also concerning the mouth of God, so that he may show that what Scripture says of the kiss of the mouth pertains to God? For either along with this he has those as well, or along with those he likewise lacks this. But indeed God has a mouth also, by which he teaches man knowledge; and he has a hand, by which he gives food to all flesh; and he has feet, whose footstool is the earth, to which, surely, the sinners of the earth, converted and humbled, make satisfaction. These, I say, God has all of them by effect, not by nature. Modest confession, surely, finds with God that to which it may cast itself down by humbling itself; and ready devotion, where it may refresh itself by being made new; and glad contemplation, where it may rest by going beyond itself. He who administers all things is all things to all, nor is he properly any one of all things. For, as to what he is in himself, he dwells in light inaccessible (1 Tim. 6:16), and his peace surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4:7); and of his wisdom there is no number (Ps. 147:5), and of his greatness there is no end (Ps. 145:3); nor can a man see him and live (Exod. 33:20). Not that he is far from any single one, he who is the being of all things, without whom all things are nothing: but, that you may wonder the more, there is nothing more present than he, and nothing more incomprehensible. For what is more present to any thing than its own being? Yet what is more incomprehensible to any than the being of all? I would indeed say that God is the being of all things, not because those things are what he is, but because from him, and through him, and in him are all things (Rom. 11:36). The being, therefore, of all things that have been made is the maker himself of them, but as cause, not as material. In such a manner, accordingly, does that majesty deign to be toward his creatures: to all, indeed, the fact that they are; to living beings, moreover, the fact that they also live; to those who use reason, light; to those who use it rightly, virtue; to those who overcome, glory.
4.5: And in creating, governing, administering, moving, carrying forward, renewing, and establishing all these things, he needs no bodily instruments, he who by his word alone created all things, both bodies and spirits. Souls need bodies and bodily senses, by which they may become known to one another and be able. But not so almighty God, to whom from the will alone a swift efficacy is at hand, as much for creating things as for ordering them as he shall have willed. He who wills is able, as much as he wills, and without the office of bodily things or the service of members. What? in order to look upon the things which he himself has made, do you think he requires for himself the aid of a bodily sense? Nothing at all of all things lies hidden, or escapes the light present everywhere; nor yet, in order that he may recognize anything, does he have need of the ministry of a sense that reports it. Nor does he only know all things without a body, but he also makes himself known without a body to the clean of heart. But I am saying the same thing more at large, that it may be plainer. But perhaps, because the straitness of a sermon that must now be ended does not allow it, it is more advisable that we put it off until tomorrow.

5.1: Four kinds of spirits are known to you: that of the beast, ours, the angelic, and he who created these. There is not one of them all for whom a body, or the likeness of a body, is not necessary, whether on his own account, or on account of another, or on account of both, except only him to whom every creature, bodily as well as spiritual, rightly confesses and says: 'You are my God, for you have no need of my goods' (Ps. 16:2). And the first, indeed, is known to need a body in such a way that it cannot in any manner even subsist without it. For at one and the same time that spirit ceases both to give life and to live, when the beast dies. But we indeed live on after the body; yet to those things by which a blessed life is lived, no access lies open for us except through the body. He had felt this who said: 'The invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made, are clearly seen' (Rom. 1:20). For the very things that have been made, that is, these bodily and visible things, come into our knowledge only as sensed through the instrument of the body. The spiritual creature which we are, therefore, has a body as something necessary, without which it surely by no means attains that knowledge which alone it has received as a step toward those things by the knowledge of which it is made blessed. If it is objected to me here concerning regenerated infants, that, departing from the body without knowledge of bodily things, they are nonetheless believed to pass over to the blessed life, I answer briefly that grace confers this upon them, not nature. And what is a miracle of God to me, who am discussing natural things?
5.2: Now, that the supercelestial spirits also have need of bodies, let that sentence make us certain above all, true and truly divine: 'Are they not all,' he says, 'ministering spirits, sent unto ministry for the sake of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation?' (Heb. 1:14.) How, then, do they fulfill their ministry without a body, especially among those who live in the body? For there is no running about, nor passing from place to place, except of bodies: which an authority as undoubted as it is well known proves that angels often do. Hence it is that they were also seen by the fathers, and entered in to them, and ate, and washed their feet. Thus the lower spirit and the higher need bodies of their own, but only such as those by which they may help, not also by which they may be helped.
5.3: But the beast, indeed, serves out of the debt of servitude, and serves by helping only for the uses of temporal and bodily necessities; and therefore that spirit both passes away with time and fails with the body. For the servant does not remain in the house forever, although those who use him well refer every use of this temporal servitude to the gain of things eternal. But the angel takes care and is busy, in the freedom of the spirit, to administer the office of piety, showing himself to mortals a ready and eager minister of good things to come, inasmuch as they are to be his fellow citizens forever and coheirs of the joy above. The one, therefore, that he may serve by right, the other that he may come to aid in piety, both without doubt need their own bodies in order to help. For in what they themselves are helped by them, I do not see, at least as regards progress toward eternity. For the irrational spirit, although he too takes in bodily things through the body: is he yet helped by his body to such a point that, through the bodily and sensible things which he senses by it, he even arrives by progress at spiritual and intelligible things? For the taking up of which, however, he is known to help, by his bodily and temporal service, those who transfer every use of temporal things to the fruit of eternal things, using this world as though not using it.
5.4: The supercelestial spirit, further, without the aid of a body and without looking upon these things which are sensed through the body, is surely sufficient, by the nearness and liveliness of his nature alone, to lay hold of the highest things and to penetrate the inmost. Did the Apostle not understand this, who, when he said, 'The invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made,' immediately added, 'from the creation of the world'? Surely because it is not so from the creature of heaven. For to that point which this spirit, wrapped in flesh and a dweller on the earth, strives by a certain gradual progress from the consideration of sensible things to arrive, little by little: to that point the inhabitant of the heavens, by his inborn fineness and loftiness, reaches with all speed and ease, supported, certainly, by no aid of a bodily sense, helped by no office of a bodily member, informed by no looking upon any bodily thing whatever. For why should he search out spiritual senses among bodies, senses which he both reads in the book of life without contradiction and understands without difficulty? why should he labor in the sweat of his face to shake grain from the chaff, wine from the grapes, and oil from the lees, when he has enough, and more than enough, of all things ready to hand? Who would beg his food through the houses of others, abounding in loaves in his own? who would take pains to dig a well, and to search out with labor the veins of water in the bowels of the earth, for whom a living fountain of its own accord pours out clear waters in abundance? Neither the brute spirit, then, nor the angelic is in any way helped by its own body toward the taking up of those things which make a creature spiritually blessed: the one, indeed, not grasping them by reason of an inborn dullness, the other not needing them by reason of the prerogative of a more excellent glory.
5.5: Further, it is manifest that the spirit of man, which holds a certain middle place between the highest and the lowest, has need of a body with respect to both, to such a degree that without it he can neither himself make progress nor be of profit to another. For, to say nothing of the other members of the body, or the offices of the members, in what way, I ask, do you either instruct one who hears, without a tongue, or perceive one who instructs, without ears?
5.6: And so, since without the aid of a body neither can the spirit of a beast pay the debt of its servile condition, nor the spiritual and heavenly creature fulfill the ministry of piety, nor the rational soul sufficiently take counsel for salvation, as much for the neighbor as also for itself: it is clear that every created spirit, whether in order to help, or in order to be helped and at the same time to help, altogether needs bodily assistance. For what if certain living creatures are found inconvenient as regards their own use, and fitted to none of the uses of human necessities? They are of profit, surely, by being seen, even if not by being used; they could be more useful to the hearts of those who look upon them than they could be to the bodies of those who use them. Even if it is agreed that they are harmful, even pernicious, to the temporal safety of men, yet their bodies do not lack that whereby they may cooperate unto good for those who have been called saints according to his purpose; and if not by yielding as food, or by showing a service, certainly by exercising the wit, in the case of him who is ready with every principle of use, unto the progress of a common discipline, by which the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made, are clearly seen. For the devil too, and his attendants, though their intent is always malignant, always desire indeed to do harm, but to those who are zealous for the good, to whom it is said, 'Who will be able to harm you, if you have been zealous for the good' (1 Pet. 3:13)? far be it that they should be able; rather they are of profit even against their will, and cooperate unto good for the good.
5.7: For the rest, whether the bodies of angels are natural to those spirits themselves, as their own are to men, and whether they are living beings as men are, yet immortal, which men are not yet; and further, whether they change and turn those very bodies into the form and appearance they wish, when they wish to appear, thickening and solidifying them as much as they wish, although in their own truth, by reason of the fineness of their nature and substance, they are impalpable and altogether unreachable by our eyes; or whether, subsisting in a simple spiritual substance, they take up bodies when there is need, and again, the work being finished, lay them aside, to be dissolved into the same matter from which they were taken: I do not wish you to require this of me. The Fathers seem to have thought differently about such things; nor is it clear to me from what source I should teach either view, and I confess that I do not know. But I also judge that knowledge of these things does not contribute much to your progress.
5.8: But know this: that none of created spirits is applied of himself to our minds, so as, with no instrument of our body or of his own intervening, to be so mingled with us or poured into us that by participation in him we should be made learned or more learned, or good or better. No angel, no soul, is in this manner capable of laying hold of me; I am capable of laying hold of none. Nor do the angels themselves lay hold of one another in this way. Let this prerogative, then, be set apart for the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit, who alone, when he teaches an angel or a man knowledge, does not seek the instrument of our bodily ear, just as neither does he seek a mouth for himself. By himself he is poured in, by himself he makes himself known; the pure is grasped by the pure. He alone needs no one; he alone is sufficient both for himself and for all, out of his almighty will alone.
5.9: Yet he works things immense and numberless through the subject creature, whether bodily or spiritual, but as one commanding, not as one begging. See, for example, that he has now taken up my bodily tongue unto his work, namely to teach you, when by himself he could without doubt do it more easily and more sweetly: it is surely an indulgence, not a need. In your progress, indeed, he seeks a merit for me, not a comfort for himself. Every man who works what is good needs to understand this same thing, lest perhaps he glory in himself concerning the goods of the Lord, and not in the Lord. There is, however, one who works what is good without willing it, whether a bad man or a bad angel: and it is clear that what is done through him is not done for his sake, since no good can be of profit to one who is unwilling. To him, therefore, only the dispensing has been entrusted; but I know not how we perceive more gratefully and more gladly the good which is ministered through an evil dispenser. This, then, is the reason why God does good things for the good even through the evil: not, however, because he needs their works in doing good.
5.10: Further, who would doubt that God needs much less those things which are without reason or sense? But when they too concur in a good work, it appears that all things serve him, to whom it belongs rightly to say, 'The world is mine' (Ps. 50:12). Or at least, because he knows what things are more fittingly done through what, he seeks from the service of the bodily creature not efficacy, but fittingness. Grant, further, that the ministries of bodies are often seasonably applied to the divine works, as, for example, rains for the quickening of seeds, or for the multiplying of crops, or for the ripening of fruits: what, I ask, has he to do with a body of his own, he to whose nod it is clear that all bodies, heavenly and earthly alike, render obedience? Plainly he would possess his own to no purpose, who finds none that is alien to him. But if we wish to conclude in the present sermon all the things which occur to be said in this place, the sermon will exceed due measure, and perhaps the strength of some: therefore let us keep what remains, to be finished under another beginning.

6.1: That the following sermon may cohere with the preceding, do you hold what was given above, that only the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit, for everything he wills to do or to have done, has no need of the instrument or the service of a body? Let us, then, securely grant to God alone, as immortality, so also incorporeity: that he alone so far transcends the whole bodily nature of spirits that he needs no body whatever in any work whatever, content, when he wills, with a spiritual nod alone, for the doing of whatever he wills. That majesty alone, therefore, is the one that has need of a bodily instrument neither on its own account nor on account of another — alone — she to whose almighty decision every work is unhesitatingly at hand, every high thing bows, every adverse thing yields, every created thing gives favor, even with no bodily or spiritual aid intervening or coming to help. He teaches or warns without a tongue; he bestows or withholds without hands; without feet he runs and runs to the help of those who are perishing.
6.2: He was doing these things also with the fathers in former ages; men experienced his attentive benefits, but the benefactor lay hidden from them. He indeed reached mightily from end to end; but, ordering all things sweetly, he was not perceived by men. And they rejoiced in the goods of the Lord; and the Lord of hosts, because he judged all things with tranquility, they did not know at all. From him they were, but not with him; through him they lived, but not unto him; from him they had wisdom, but not him, alienated, ungrateful, without sense. Hence at last it came about that what they were, that they lived, that they had wisdom, they did not attribute to the author, but ascribed to nature, or indeed, what was more foolish, to fortune; and many arrogated many things also to their own industry and virtue. How much did seducing spirits usurp for themselves, how much was given to the sun and the moon; how much was attributed to the earth and the waters, how much even assigned to the handmade and fabricated works of mortals! To herbs, to shrubs, to the tiniest and vilest seeds, reverence was paid as to divinities.
6.3: Alas! have men thus lost and exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats hay? (Ps. 106:20.) Their errors God pitied, and, graciously coming forth from the shady and thick-covered mountain, he set his tabernacle in the sun (Ps. 19:5). He offered flesh to those who were wise as to the flesh, through which they might learn to be wise also as to the spirit. For while in the flesh and through the flesh he does works not of the flesh but of God, commanding nature, surely, and overcoming fortune, making foolish the wisdom of men, and conquering the tyranny of demons, he manifestly shows that he himself is the one through whom those same things were done before also, when they were done. In the flesh, I say, and through the flesh, working wonders mightily and openly, speaking things wholesome, suffering things unworthy, he evidently shows that he himself is the one who had mightily, but invisibly, founded the ages, wisely rules them, and kindly protects them. Finally, while he preaches the gospel to the ungrateful, gives signs to unbelievers, and prays for his crucifiers: does he not clearly declare that he himself is the one who, with his Father, daily makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust? (Matt. 5:45.) For this is what he himself was saying: 'If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe' (John 10:37).
6.4: See, he opens the mouth of his flesh, teaching the disciples on the mountain, he who in silence teaches the angels in the heavens. See, at the touch of his bodily hand leprosy is cured, blindness is put to flight, hearing is restored, the mute tongue is loosed, the disciple nearly sunk is raised up; and he is recognized without doubt as the one to whom David had said long before: 'You open your hand, and fill every living thing with blessing' (Ps. 145:16); and again: 'When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness' (Ps. 104:28). See, the sinner lying beside his bodily feet and repenting hears: 'Your sins are forgiven you' (Luke 7:48), and she recognizes him of whom, from many ages back, she had read that it was written: 'The devil will go forth before his feet' (Hab. 3:5). For where sin is forgiven, there without doubt the devil is driven out of the sinner's heart. Hence he says universally of all who repent: 'Now is the judgment of the world, now the prince of this world will be cast out' (John 12:31): namely, that God forgives sin to the one who humbly confesses, and the devil loses the dominion which he had seized in the heart of man.
6.5: Finally he walks upon the waves with fleshly feet (Matt. 14:25), he of whom, not yet clothed with flesh, the Psalmist had already sung beforehand: 'In the sea is your way, and your paths in many waters'; which is: you trample the swelling hearts of the proud, and you press down the fluid desires of carnal men, justifying the ungodly and humbling the proud. But because this is done invisibly, the carnal man does not perceive by whom it is done. And therefore he adds: 'And your footsteps will not be known' (Ps. 77:19). Hence again the Father to the Son: 'Sit,' he says, 'at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet' (Ps. 110:1); that is: until I subject to your will all who despise you, whether unwilling and wretched, or willing and blessed. And so, because the flesh was not perceiving this work of the Spirit (for the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14), it was needful that the sinner, lying bodily upon his bodily feet and kissing those same feet with bodily lips, should receive the pardon of her sins; and that thus that change of the right hand of the Most High (Ps. 77:10), by which he wonderfully but invisibly justifies the ungodly, should become known even to carnal men.
6.6: But those spiritual feet of God, which the penitent ought in the first place to kiss spiritually, it does not behoove me to pass over. I know your curiosity, which of its own will would pass over nothing at all that has been left unexplained. Nor indeed is it to be held in contempt to know the feet with which Scripture so often mentions God, now indeed as standing, as there: 'We will worship in the place where his feet stood' (Ps. 132:7); now as walking, as there: 'And I will dwell in them, and walk about among them' (Lev. 26:12; 2 Cor. 6:16); now even as running, according to that word: 'He has exulted as a giant to run his course' (Ps. 19:5). If it seemed right to the Apostle to refer the head of Christ to the Godhead (1 Cor. 11:3), I think it will not seem unfitting to us either that the feet pertain to the man, of which let us name the one mercy and the other judgment. These two words are known to you; and from very many places of Scripture both occur together, if you consider. But that God took up the foot of mercy in the flesh to which he united himself, the epistle to the Hebrews teaches, declaring Christ tempted in all things after our likeness, yet without sin, that he might become merciful (Heb. 4:15). What of that other, which has been named judgment: does not the God-man himself openly signify that it too pertains equally to the man who was assumed, where he declares that power to execute judgment has been given him by the Father, because he is the Son of man? (John 5:27.)
6.7: With these two feet, then, fittingly running together under the one head of the divinity, Emmanuel, invisible, born of a woman, made under the law, was seen upon earth and conversed with men (Bar. 3:38). With these, certainly, he passes through even now, doing good and healing all who are oppressed by the devil, yet spiritually, yet invisibly. With these feet, I say, he walks through devout minds, unceasingly surveying and searching the hearts and reins of the faithful. But see whether these are not perhaps those legs of the bridegroom which the bride so magnificently commends in what follows, comparing them, if I am not mistaken, to columns of marble founded upon bases of gold (Song 5:15). Altogether beautifully; since indeed in the incarnate Wisdom of God, which is signified by the gold, mercy and truth have met one another (Ps. 85:10); and finally, all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 25:10).
6.8: Happy the mind in which the Lord Jesus has once fixed both feet! By two signs recognize the soul that is of this sort, which must bear within herself the marks impressed by the divine footsteps. They are fear and hope, the one presenting the image of judgment, the other of mercy. Rightly is the Lord well pleased with those who fear him, and with those who hope in his mercy (Ps. 147:11): since fear is the beginning of wisdom (Prov. 1:7); hope, its progress: for charity claims the consummation for herself. Since these things are so, the fruit is no small one in this first kiss, which is received at the feet; only take care that you are deprived of neither of them. For if already you are pricked by sorrow for sin and by fear of judgment, you have pressed your lips to the footprint of truth and of judgment. But if, by looking upon the divine goodness and by the hope of obtaining pardon, you temper the fear and the sorrow, know that you also embrace the foot of mercy. Otherwise it is not expedient to kiss the one without the other; for the remembrance of judgment alone hurls one headlong into the abyss of despair, and a deceitful assent to mercy begets the worst security.
6.9: It has been granted to me also, a wretch, sometimes to sit beside the feet of the Lord Jesus, and to embrace now this one, now that, with entire devotion, insofar as his kindness has deigned to admit me. But if ever, forgetful of pity, and with conscience stinging me, I clung a little too long to judgment, soon cast down by an incredible fear and a miserable confusion, and wrapped in a dark horror, panting out this alone I cried from the depths: 'Who knows the power of your anger, and for fear of you to number your wrath?' (Ps. 90:11, 12.) But if, leaving that foot, it happened that I held more to the foot of mercy, I was on the contrary so loosened by carelessness and negligence that at once prayer appeared more lukewarm, action more sluggish, laughter readier, speech less cautious, and finally the whole state of both the inward and the outward man more inconstant. Instructed, therefore, by experience as my teacher, I will now sing to you, Lord, not judgment alone, or mercy alone, but mercy and judgment together (Ps. 101:1). Forever I will not forget these justifications of yours; both alike will be songs for me in the place of my pilgrimage, until mercy, exalted above judgment, misery falls silent, and my glory alone sings to you henceforth, and I am not pricked with compunction.

7.1: I stir up labor for myself, I who of my own accord provoke you to inquiry. For because, on the occasion of the first kiss, I took care to point out the spiritual feet of God by definitions and names of their own, and that indeed more than was needed, you go on to inquire also about the hand, which is proposed to be kissed in the second place. I assent, I comply with your wish; and more than that, I show not a hand but hands, and I distinguish them by names of their own. Let the one be called largesse, the other strength: because he both gives abundantly, and powerfully defends what he has given. He will surely kiss each of them who has not been ungrateful, recognizing and confessing God as both the lavish giver of all good things and their keeper. I think enough has been said of the two kisses: let us look also at the third.
7.2: 'Let him kiss me,' she says, 'with the kiss of his mouth' (Song 1:1). Who says it? The bride. And who is she herself? The soul thirsting for God. But I set down different affections, so that the one which properly belongs to the bride may shine out more distinctly. If he is a servant, he fears from the face of the Lord; if a hireling, he hopes from the hand of the Lord; if a disciple, he readies his ear for the master; if a son, he honors the father; but she who asks for a kiss, loves. This affection of love excels among the gifts of nature, especially when it runs back to its own beginning, which is God. Nor have names equally sweet been found by which the sweet affections of the Word and the soul toward one another might be expressed, as bridegroom and bride: for to these all things are common, and they have nothing of their own, nothing divided from one another. One inheritance of both, one house, one table, one bed, even one flesh. For on this account he will leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be in one flesh (Gen. 2:24). She also is bidden no less to forget her people and her father's house, so that he may desire her beauty (Ps. 45:10, 11). If, then, to love belongs especially and principally to spouses, not unfittingly is the soul that loves designated by the name of bride. But she loves who asks for a kiss. She does not ask freedom, not a wage, not an inheritance, nor finally even teaching, but a kiss; plainly in the manner of a most chaste bride, breathing a sacred love, and altogether unable to disguise the flame which she suffers. For see what a beginning of speech she seizes upon. About to ask a great thing from the great one, she nevertheless uses none of the paint of flatteries, as is usual; she approaches what she desires by no roundabout ways. She makes no preface, she does not court goodwill; but breaking out suddenly from the abundance of the heart, plainly and boldly enough: 'Let him kiss me,' she says, 'with the kiss of his mouth.'
7.3: Does she not seem to you to be saying, as it were, openly: 'What is there for me in heaven, and besides you what have I wished for upon earth?' (Ps. 73:25.) She loves chastely, surely, who seeks him whom she loves, and not anything else of his. She loves holily, because not in the concupiscence of the flesh, but in the purity of the spirit. She loves ardently, who is so drunk with her own love that she does not consider the majesty. What then? he looks upon the earth and makes it tremble (Ps. 104:32); and she demands to be kissed by him! Is she drunk? Utterly drunk. And perhaps then, when she broke out into these words, she had come forth from the wine cellar, into which she afterward glories that she was brought (Song 1:3; 2:4). For David also said to God of certain ones: 'They shall be made drunk with the plenty of your house, and you will give them to drink of the torrent of your pleasure' (Ps. 36:8). O how great is the force of love! how great the confidence in the spirit of liberty! What is more manifest than that perfect charity casts fear outside? (1 John 4:18.)
7.4: Yet modestly she does not direct her speech to the bridegroom himself, but to others, as though concerning one who is absent: 'Let him kiss me,' she says, 'with the kiss of his mouth.' For a great thing is asked, and there is need that modesty accompany the prayer and commend the one who asks. And so through the members of the household and the intimates, access to the inner places is sought, and an approach to the thing desired is solicited. Who, then, are they? We believe that the holy angels stand by those who pray, and offer to God the prayers and vows of men, yet only where they have seen pure hands lifted up without anger and contention. The angel proves this, speaking thus to Tobias: 'When you were praying with tears, and burying the dead, and leaving your dinner, and hiding the dead by day in your house, and burying them by night, I offered your prayer to the Lord' (Tob. 12:12). I think this is sufficiently established for you from other testimonies of Scripture as well. For that the holy angels are also wont to mingle graciously with those who sing psalms, what is more manifest than that the Psalmist says: 'The princes went before, joined with the singers, in the midst of young women playing timbrels'? (Ps. 68:25.) Whence he also said: 'In the sight of the angels I will sing psalms to you' (Ps. 138:1). I grieve, accordingly, that some of you are weighed down by heavy sleep in the sacred vigils, and do not revere the citizens of heaven, but appear as dead men in the presence of princes, when they themselves, moved by your eagerness, delight to take part in your solemnities. I fear lest, at some time abominating your sloth, they withdraw with indignation, and each one of you begin too late to say to God with a groan. 'You have put my acquaintances far from me; they have made me an abomination to themselves'; and that: 'You have removed friend and neighbor far from me, and my acquaintances because of misery' (Ps. 88:8, 18); likewise: 'Those who were near me stood afar off, and those who sought my life used violence' (Ps. 38:11, 12). For certainly, if the good spirits have removed themselves far from us, who will withstand the onset of the malignant? I say, therefore, to those who are of this sort: 'Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently' (Jer. 48:10). He says also — not I, but the Lord: 'Would that I had found you hot or cold! but because I have found you lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth' (Rev. 3:15, 16). For this reason give heed to your princes when you stand to pray or to sing psalms, and stand with reverence and discipline; and glory, because your angels daily see the face of the Father (Matt. 18:10). For, sent unto ministry for our sake, who are to receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb. 1:14), they carry our devotion to the heights and bring grace back. Let us take up the office of those whose fellowship we obtain by lot, so that praise may be perfected in the mouth of infants and of nursing children (Ps. 8:2). Let us say to them: 'Sing psalms to our God, sing psalms'; and let us hear them answering in turn: 'Sing psalms to our King, sing psalms.'
7.5: Leading praise, then, in common with the singers of heaven, inasmuch as you are fellow citizens of the saints and members of the household of God, sing psalms wisely (Ps. 47:6, 7). Food has savor in the mouth; a psalm, in the heart. Only let the faithful and prudent soul not neglect to chew it with certain teeth of her understanding, lest, if she happen to swallow it whole and unchewed, the palate be cheated of the desirable taste, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Let us offer, with the apostles, at the heavenly banquet and at the Lord's table, a honeycomb (Luke 24:42). The honey is in the wax; the devotion is in the letter. Otherwise the letter kills, if you swallow it without the seasoning of the spirit (2 Cor. 3:6). But if, with the Apostle, you sing psalms with the spirit, sing psalms also with the mind (1 Cor. 14:15); you too will recognize the truth of that word which Jesus spoke: 'The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life' (John 6:63); and likewise of that which we read, Wisdom saying: 'My spirit is sweet above honey' (Sir. 24:27).
7.6: Thus will your soul delight in fatness, thus will your burnt offering be made rich. Thus will you make the king favorable, thus will you please the princes, thus finally will you render the whole court well disposed toward you; and, having scented the odor of sweetness in the heavens, they will say of you also: 'Who is she that ascends through the desert, like a little pillar of smoke, from the aromas of myrrh and frankincense and of every powder of the perfumer' (Song 3:6)? 'Princes,' he says, 'of Judah, their leaders, princes of Zebulun, princes of Naphtali' (Ps. 68:27); that is, of those who confess, of those who are continent, of those who contemplate. For our princes know that acceptable to their King are the confession of those who sing psalms, the fortitude of the continent, and the purity of those who contemplate: and they are solicitous to require of us firstfruits of the spirit of this kind, which surely are nothing other than the first and purest fruits of wisdom. For, as you are not ignorant, Judah is interpreted 'praising' or 'confessing,' Zebulun 'a dwelling of strength,' and Naphtali 'a hind let loose': which, surely, by the leaps of its agility expresses the ecstasies of one who gazes, and is also accustomed to penetrate the shady places of the groves, as that one the shady places of the senses. But we know who it was that said: 'The sacrifice of praise will honor me' (Ps. 50:23).
7.7: But if praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Sir. 15:9), do you not have a most necessary need of the virtue of continence, through which it may come about that sin does not reign in your mortal body? Further, continence has no merit with God when it seeks human glory. And therefore there is most of all need also of purity of intention, by which your mind may both desire to please God alone and be able to cling to him. For to cling to God is nothing other than to see God, which is granted, by a singular happiness, to the clean of heart alone. David had a clean heart, who said to God: 'My soul has clung close after you' (Ps. 63:8); and again: 'But for me it is good to cling to God' (Ps. 73:28). By seeing he clung, and by clinging he saw. Souls exercised in these things, therefore, the messengers of heaven show themselves familiar with, and frequent, especially if they have perceived one praying often. Who will grant me, through you, O kindly princes, to make my petitions known with God? Not to God, to whom even the thought of man confesses, but with God; that is, to those who are with God, the blessed powers as well as the spirits loosed from the flesh. Who will raise me up from the earth, needy, and lift the poor man from the dunghill, that I may sit with princes and hold a throne of glory? I do not doubt that they gladly gather into the palace the one whom they graciously visit on the dunghill. For they have rejoiced over the conversion: and in the taking up, will they not acknowledge him?
7.8: These, then, I think the bride addresses while she prays, and to them, as to the household companions and comrades of the bridegroom, she opens the desire of her heart, when she says: 'Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.' And see the familiar and friendly conversation of a soul sighing in the flesh with the heavenly powers. She is eager for kisses, she asks what she longs for; yet she does not name the one she loves, because she does not doubt that they know him, inasmuch as she is accustomed to have frequent conversation with them about him. For this reason she does not say: 'Let this one or that one kiss me'; but only: 'Let him kiss me'; just as Mary Magdalene also did not express by name the one she was seeking, but only said to him whom she thought the gardener: 'Lord, if you have taken him away' (John 20:15). Whom, him? She does not disclose it, because she believes it is plain to all, that which cannot depart from her heart even for a moment. So, then, she also, speaking to the comrades of her bridegroom, as to those who share the secret and to whom she knew herself to be manifest, the name left unspoken, suddenly breaks out into these words about the beloved: 'Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.' Concerning this kiss I do not now wish to keep you longer, but in tomorrow's sermon you will hear whatever the anointing that teaches concerning all things shall deign to suggest to me about it, as you pray. For flesh and blood do not reveal this secret, but he who searches the deep things of God, the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from the Father and the Son, with them equally lives and reigns unto ages of ages. Amen.

8.1: Today, as you hold from yesterday's promise, it is proposed to discuss with you the highest kiss, that is, the kiss of the mouth. Hear more attentively what tastes sweeter, is tasted more rarely, and is understood with more difficulty. It seems to me, that I may begin a little higher, that he designated a certain kiss ineffable and unexperienced by every creature, who says: 'No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, or he to whom the Son shall have willed to reveal him' (Matt. 11:27).
