Then see also lest you do not wholly resign his gifts to God, and, bending something of his glory and honor back to yourself, you be deservedly accused of fraud, and of fraud against God. For if, of these things of which you boast, you were perhaps claiming something for yourself from yourself, I would believe that you were deceived rather than that you wished to defraud, and I would correct the error. But now, because by giving thanks you prove that you attribute nothing to yourself, but that your merits are the gifts of God, that you acknowledge this prudently, by despising the rest you certainly betray that you have spoken what is in the heart, and with the heart: lending one of them to a lie, and with the other usurping the glory of the truth. For you would not judge the publican to be despised in comparison with yourself, if you did not consider yourself to be honored in comparison with him. But what do you answer the Apostle, who prescribes and says: 'To God alone be honor and glory'? (1 Tim. 1:17.) What do you answer the angel, who distinguishes and teaches what God is pleased to keep for himself, and what he deigns to share with men? For: 'Glory,' he says, 'to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will' (Luke 2:14). Do you not see the Pharisee, while giving thanks, honoring God indeed with the lips, but himself by the sentence of the heart? Thus it is to be noticed that thanksgiving sounds in the mouth of many by a kind of habit rather than by sense or affection, to such a degree that even the most wicked men are accustomed to give thanks to God for each of their crimes and outrages, because it has turned out well and prosperously for them, as they themselves indeed judge, in the fulfilling of their perverse wills. You may hear, for example, a thief, when he has carried off the wickedly desired handful of an impious plot, exulting in secret and saying: 'Thanks be to God, I have not kept vain watches, I have not lost my night's labor.' Likewise, he who has killed a man, does he not glory, and return thanks, that he has prevailed against a rival, or avenged himself upon an enemy? And no less does the adulterer dance and exult in the praises of God, that he has at last obtained the intercourse long desired.
13.3: Not every thanksgiving, then, is acceptable to God, but only that which proceeds from a chaste and pure simplicity of heart. Chaste, I would say, on account of those who, glorying even in their evil deeds, are accustomed to give thanks to God, as if God, after their manner, rejoiced when they have done evil, and exulted in the worst things. He who is of this sort will hear: 'You have thought wickedly that I shall be like you; I will reprove you, and set it before your face' (Ps. 50:21). But I added 'pure' on account of the hypocrites, who indeed glorify God for their good things, but in word only, and keep back in the heart what they had offered with the mouth; and because they act deceitfully in his sight, their iniquity is found unto hatred. The former impiously twist their own evils to God; the latter fraudulently twist the goods of God to themselves. And indeed that first thing is so foolish, and so worldly, and in a certain way even beastly, that I have no need to warn you about it: but the following one is accustomed to lie in wait especially for religious and spiritual men. It is surely a great and rare virtue that, although you do great things, you should not know yourself to be great, and that your holiness, manifest to all, should lie hidden from you alone. To appear wonderful, and to repute yourself contemptible: this I judge more wonderful than the virtues themselves. You are a faithful servant indeed, if of the great glory of your Lord, even though it does not go out from you, yet passes through you, it happens that nothing sticks to your hands. Then, according to the prophet, you cast avarice out of extortion, and you shake your hands free from every gift (Isa. 33:15). Then, according to the command of the Lord, your light shines before men, unto the glorifying not of you, but of the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16). But also, an imitator of Paul and of the faithful preachers, who do not preach themselves, you likewise do not seek the things that are your own, but the things that are Jesus Christ's (2 Cor. 4:5; Phil. 2:21). Wherefore you also will hear: 'Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many' (Matt. 25:21).
13.4: Joseph, when he knew that the house and all the goods of his Egyptian master had been entrusted to him, did not fail to know that the mistress was excepted; and on this account he did not consent to touch her. 'There is nothing,' he says, 'of all the goods of my master that is not in my power, or that he has not handed over to me, except you, who are his wife' (Gen. 39:9). He had known that the woman is the glory of the man, and he judged it unjust for himself, by a contrary exchange, to make inglorious him who had made him glorious. The man of God, prudent in wisdom, noticed that a husband jealously guards his wife as his own glory, and has kept her to be preserved for himself, not entrusted her to another; and he did not presume to stretch out his hand to what had not been granted. What then? A man is jealous for his own glory, and does God dare to wish to defraud him of his, as though he were not jealous? But hear what he says: 'My glory,' he says, 'I will not give to another' (Isa. 48:11). What, then, will you give, O Lord, what will you give us? 'Peace,' he says, 'I give you; peace I leave you' (John 14:27). It is enough for me: I gratefully receive what you leave, and I leave what you keep. So it pleases, so I do not doubt that it concerns me. I renounce glory utterly, lest perhaps, if I usurp what has not been granted, I deservedly lose what has been offered as well. I want peace, I desire peace, and nothing more. He for whom peace is not enough, you are not enough for him. For you are our peace, who have made both one (Eph. 2:14). This is necessary for me, this is enough: to be reconciled to you, to be reconciled to myself. For from the time you set me as an adversary to yourself, I have become heavy also to myself (Job 7:20). I am cautious, that I may be neither ungrateful for the benefit of the peace that has been given, nor a sacrilegious invader of your glory. To you, O Lord, to you let your glory remain undiminished; it is well with me if I have peace.
13.5: When Goliath had been laid low, the people rejoiced in the peace they had received, but David stood out as glorious in a singular way. Joshua, Jephthah, Gideon, Samson, and Judith also, although a woman, triumphed gloriously in their days over their enemies; but while the rest enjoyed peace with joy, no one shared with them in the glory. Judas Maccabeus, himself also renowned for many victories, when by fighting bravely he had often granted peace to an exulting people, did he ever share the glory with anyone? Finally it is said, 'And there was,' not glory, but 'great joy among the people' (1 Macc. 4:58). What less than all these has the Maker of all done, that he too should not be bound to glory in a singular way? He alone created all things, he alone triumphed over the enemy, he alone set the captives free: and will he have a partner in the glory? 'And my arm,' he says, 'has helped me'; and again: 'I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there is no man with me' (Isa. 63:5, 3). What, then, have I to do with the victory, if I was not even in the battle? Most impudently do I claim for myself either glory without victory, or victory without a fight. But receive, O mountains, peace for the people; receive peace for yourselves, not glory, keeping it for him alone who alone both fought and conquered. So, I ask, so let it be: 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.' But he is of a will not good, but plainly wicked, who, by no means content with peace, restless with a proud eye and an insatiable heart, pants also after the glory of God, and therefore neither keeps the peace nor lays hold of the glory. Who would believe a wall, if it said that it was giving birth to the ray which it receives through the window? or if the clouds should glory that they had begotten the rains, who would not laugh? It is clearly established for me that neither are streams of water drawn out of channels, nor words of prudence out of lips or teeth, even if a bodily sense reaches no further.
13.6: If I look upon anything in the saints worthy of praise or admiration, discussing it in the clear light of truth, I surely find that one appears praiseworthy or wonderful, and that another is so: and I praise God in his saints, whether it be Elisha, or that great Elijah, raisers, certainly, of the dead. They themselves, indeed, not by their own command but by their ministry, display outwardly to us things new and unusual; but God, remaining in them, himself does the works. Invisible and inaccessible in himself, in his own he is to be seen and wondered at, and he alone is wonderful, who alone does wonderful things (Ps. 72:18). Nor is the pen praiseworthy for a picture or a writing that is praiseworthy; nor is a good word the glory of the tongue or the lips. It is time that the prophet also should speak. 'Will the axe,' he says, 'glory against him who cuts with it? or shall the saw be exalted against him by whom it is drawn?' As if a rod should be lifted up against him who lifts it, and the staff be exalted, which is surely wood (Isa. 10:15): so is everyone against the Lord who glories, if he does not glory in the Lord (2 Cor. 10:17). If there is to be glorying, Paul has taught me from what, and in what. 'This,' he says, 'is our glory, the testimony of our conscience' (2 Cor. 1:12). I glory securely, if, with conscience as witness, I usurp for myself nothing of the glory of the Creator; securely, plainly, because now it is not against the Lord, but in the Lord. This glorying is not only not forbidden us, but is even urged, when it is said: 'You seek glory from one another, and the glory which is from God alone you do not want' (John 5:44). Truly, to glory in God alone is from God alone. Nor is this glory a slight one, being as true as it is from the truth, and in the truth so rare that scarcely even a few of the perfect glory perfectly in it. Let the vain sons of men go, then, the lying sons of men; let them go, and let them deceive one another from vanity unto the same thing (Ps. 62:9). For the wise man who glories will prove his own work, and will examine it diligently by the light of truth; and so he will have glory in himself, and not in the mouth of another. I am a fool if I entrust my glory to the little basket of your lips, and begin to beg it from you when I wish to have it. Is it not, surely, in your choice to approve me or to disapprove me, as you will? But I keep it in my own possession; I myself keep it more faithfully for myself. Or rather, I do not even entrust it to myself: I lay it up rather to be kept by him who is able to keep my deposit unto that day (2 Tim. 1:12), careful in guarding it, faithful in restoring it. Then the praise of each one will be secure from God, at least for those who have despised human praises. For glory is in the confusion of those who mind earthly things, David saying also: 'Those who please men have been confounded, because God has despised them' (Ps. 53:5).
13.7: Brethren, if you know these things, let none of you wish to be praised in this life; because whatever of favor you catch at here which you have not referred to God, you steal from him. For you, whence is glory, O rotting dust, for you whence? From holiness of life? But it is the Spirit who sanctifies, the Spirit, I say, not your own, but the Spirit of God. Even if you shine out with prodigies and signs, they are done in your hand, but by the power of God. Or does popular favor flatter you, because you have brought forth a good word, and perhaps brought it forth well? But Christ has given mouth and wisdom. For what is your tongue but the pen of a scribe? And this very thing you have received on loan. A talent has been entrusted, to be demanded back with interest. If you have been found diligent for the work, faithful in returning the fruit, you will receive a reward for your labor. If otherwise, the talent will be taken from you, and the profit will nonetheless be exacted, and you will be called a wicked and slothful servant. Let every praise, then, for the goods of the manifold grace appearing in you be referred to him, the author and lavish giver, surely, of all things praiseworthy; and that not feignedly, as by hypocrites, nor by habit alone, as by worldly men; nor even by necessity, as beasts are applied to the bearing of burdens: but as befits the saints, with a faithful sincerity, a solicitous devotion, a grateful cheerfulness, yet not a loose one. Offering, then, the sacrifice of praise, and paying our vows from day to day, let us take care with all watchfulness to join sense to use, affection to sense, exultation to affection, gravity to exultation, humility to gravity, liberty to humility: so that at times we may go forward with the free steps of a purged mind, and pass beyond, through certain unaccustomed spiritual affections, into jubilant delights, in the light of God, in sweetness, in the Holy Spirit; proving that we have been laid hold of among those whom the prophet was looking at when he said, 'Lord, in the light of your countenance they shall walk, and in your name they shall exult all the day, and in your justice they shall be exalted' (Ps. 89:15, 16).
13.8: But perhaps someone may say to me: 'You admonish well, but if only you were saying things that fitted your purpose.' Wait a little; I am not unmindful. Is it not in our hands to treat of that which is said, 'Your name is oil poured out'? (Song 1:2.) This is the work, this the labor. And whether the things we set down beforehand were necessary, you yourselves will see. Now, as far as I am concerned, that they are not foreign to this, attend in a few words. Do you not remember that in the breasts of the bride the sweet odor of the ointments was commended last? What, then, is more consistent than that the bride should acknowledge the same fragrance as from the benefit of the bridegroom, lest she be thought to claim it for herself? To which sense, plainly, you recognize that all those things which we have set down beforehand are subservient. 'That my breasts,' she says, 'breathe so, and so please, I ascribe neither to my studies nor to my merits, but I attribute it to your largesse, O bridegroom; from the oil, surely, that has been poured out, your name.' This for the sequence of the letter.
13.9: But the explanation of the chapter itself, on the occasion of which we have drawn out the present sermon to such length upon the most wicked vice of ingratitude, requires another time and another beginning of the sermon. Now let it suffice that you have been admonished of this only: if the bride, surely, by no means dares to claim anything for herself of all her virtue or grace, how much less the young maidens, who perhaps are what we are? Let us say, then, we also, following the footsteps of the bride, let us say: 'Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give the glory' (Ps. 115:1). Let us say it not in word and tongue only, but in work and truth, lest perhaps (which I fear too much) it be said of us also: 'Because they loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him; but their heart was not right with him, nor were they held faithful in his covenant' (Ps. 78:36, 37). Let us say, then, let us say, crying out from the marrow of the heart more than from the lips of the mouth: 'Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from the nations, that we may confess your holy name, not our own; and may glory in your praise, not ours, but yours' (Ps. 106:47), unto ages of ages. Amen.

14.1: God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel (Ps. 76:1). The people of the nations who were walking in darkness have seen a great light (Isa. 9:2), which was in Judah and in Israel, and they wished to draw near and be enlightened, so that those who once were not a people might now be a people (1 Pet. 2:10); and one cornerstone might receive into itself both walls coming from opposite sides, and thenceforth his place might be in peace. Further, confidence was given by the voice of the one inviting, which had already sounded. 'Rejoice, you nations, with his people' (Deut. 32:43; Rom. 15:10). She wished, then, to draw near; but the Synagogue forbade it, asserting that the Church from the nations was unclean and unworthy, casting at her the dregs of idolatry and the blindness of ignorance, and she was saying: 'You, indeed, by what merit?' Do not touch me. Why, she says? Is God the God of the Jews only? is he not also of the Gentiles? (Rom. 3:29.) And if merit is certainly lacking to me, mercy is not lacking to him. Is he only just? He is also merciful. 'Let your mercies come to me, O Lord, and I shall live'; and again: 'Many are your mercies, O Lord; according to your judgment give me life' (Ps. 119:77, 156); which, tempered, surely, is mercy. What will the Lord, just and merciful, do, the one glorying in the law and applauding righteousness to herself, and not needing mercy, but despising her who does need it; the other, on the contrary, acknowledging her own offenses, confessing her unworthiness, refusing judgment, demanding mercy? what, I say, will the judge do, and that judge to whom both to judge and to have mercy are so familiar that neither is more familiar than the other? What, surely, could be more fitting than that each should receive according to her own wish, that one judgment, this one mercy? The Jew seeks judgment, and let her have it; but let the nations honor God for his mercy. And the judgment is this: that those who despise the merciful justice of God, and wish to establish their own (which surely does not justify, but accuses), should be left to that righteousness of their own, to be crushed rather than justified.
14.2: For there is a righteousness from the law, which has never led anyone to perfection; there is a yoke which neither they nor their fathers were ever able to bear. But the Synagogue is strong; she does not care for a light burden or a sweet yoke. She is healthy; she has no need of a physician, nor of the anointing of the Spirit. She trusts in the law; let it set her free if it can. But the law was not given which is able to give life, and moreover it kills: for the letter kills (2 Cor. 3:6). 'Therefore,' he says, 'I say to you: you will die in your sins' (John 8:24). This, then, O Synagogue, is the judgment which you demand for your error. Blind and contentious, you are abandoned, until the fullness of the nations (which you proudly spurn and enviously drive away) comes in, and she also herself acknowledges him, that God is known in Judah, and that his name is great in Israel. For to this judgment Jesus came into this world: that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind (John 9:39). In part, however; because the Lord will not cast off his people (Ps. 94:14), keeping for himself, out of the whole, as a seed the apostles and the multitude of believers, whose heart was one and whose soul was one. But neither will he cast them off unto the end, being about to save a remnant. For he will again receive Israel his child, and will remember his mercy (Luke 1:54), so that not even there does mercy, as a companion, abandon judgment, where she herself finds no place. Otherwise, if he had received them according to their merits, there would surely be judgment without mercy for him who does not do mercy (James 2:13). For Judah has much oil of the divine knowledge, and she keeps it greedily within herself, shut up as in a vessel. I ask, and she does not pity, nor does she lend. She alone wishes to possess the worship of God, she alone the knowledge, she alone his great name; nor is she jealous for herself, but she envies me.
14.3: You, then, O Lord, judge my judgment, and let your great name be magnified still, and let the oil which is much be multiplied more. Let it grow, let it boil over, let it be poured out, let it be channeled even to the nations, and let all flesh feel the salvation of God. How is it that the ungrateful Jew wishes the whole saving anointing to remain in the beard of Aaron? It belongs not to the beard, but to the head. But the head belongs not to the beard alone, but also to the whole body. Let her receive it first, surely, but not alone. Let her pour back upon the lower members what she herself has received from above. Let the liquor from above descend, let it descend even to the breasts of the Church (for, too greedy, she does not scorn to press this out for herself from the beard); and, steeped in the dew of grace, that she may prove herself not ungrateful, let her say: 'Your name is oil poured out' (Song 1:2). But let it overflow still, I ask, and reach even to the hem of the garment, to me, surely, the last of all and the most unworthy, yet of the garment. For I also demand that for myself from the mother's breasts, as a little one in Christ, by the right, surely, of piety. But if the man murmurs, whose eye is evil because of the goodness, answer for me, O Lord; let my judgment come forth from your face, and not from the eyebrow of Israel. Rather answer for yourself, and say to the calumniator — for he brings a charge against you, that you give freely — say to him, then: 'I will, and to this last one I will give likewise' (Matt. 20:14). It displeases the Pharisee. Why do you mutter? My right is the will of the judge. What is more just as to merit, what richer as to reward? Is it not lawful for him to do what he wills? To me, indeed, mercy is done, but to you no injury at all. Take what is yours, and go. If he has determined to save me also, what do you lose?
14.4: Heap up your merits as much as you will, and extol your sweats: the mercy of the Lord is better than lives (Ps. 63:3). I confess I have not borne the burden of the day and the heat; but I carry a sweet yoke and a light burden, according to the good pleasure of the householder. My work is scarcely of one hour; and if more, I do not feel it, for love. Let the Jew exercise his own strength; I am pleased to prove what is the will of the Lord, good, and pleasing, and perfect. From that, surely, I repair for myself the losses of work and of time. He relies on the bargain of a contract; I, on the good pleasure of the will: I believe, and not unto folly for myself, for life is in his will. That reconciles the Father to me, that restores the inheritance, even with a more abundant grace; it raises up for me the music, and the song, and the banquets, and the most celebrated joys of the whole exulting household. If my elder brother is indignant, he who prefers to eat a kid with his friends outside rather than the fatted calf with me in the father's house, it will be answered him: 'It is fitting to feast and to rejoice, because this my son was dead, and has come to life again; he was lost, and is found' (Luke 15:32). The Synagogue still feasts outside with her friends the demons, whom it pleases well enough that, foolish, she devours the kid of sin, swallowing it down, and in a certain way hiding it and storing it up for herself in the belly of her sluggishness and her folly, while, despising the justice of God and wishing to establish her own, she says that she has no sin, and has no need of the death of the fatted calf, reputing herself clean and just from the works of the law. But the Church, the veil of the killing letter having been torn in the death of the crucified Word, boldly bursts into his inner places, the spirit of liberty going before, is acknowledged, pleases, obtains the place of her rival, becomes the bride, enjoys the embraces she has seized beforehand; and, clinging in the heat of the spirit to Christ the Lord, against whom she is pressed, receiving this oil of his exultation as it drips and pours from every side, she above her companions, says: 'Your name is oil poured out.' What wonder if she is anointed, who embraces the Anointed?
14.5: The Church, then, reclines within, but for the time being the Church of the perfect. Yet there is hope for us also. Let us who are less perfect keep watch before the doors, rejoicing in hope. Let the bridegroom and the bride alone be within for the time being, let them enjoy mutual and secret embraces, with no noise of carnal desires, no tumult of bodily phantasms disturbing them. But the crowd of young maidens, who cannot yet be without restlessness of this sort, let them wait outside; and let them wait securely, knowing that what they read looks to themselves: 'Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her neighbors shall be brought to you' (Ps. 45:14). And that each may know of what spirit she is, I mean those virgins who, espoused to Christ before they were defiled by the embraces of the world, persevere firmly in him to whom they vowed themselves the more happily the earlier they did so; but the neighbors, those who, at last at some time blushing for their former deformity, in which, once conformed to this world, they had shamefully prostituted themselves to the princes of the world, that is, to unclean spirits, in every carnal concupiscence, and coming out of it, hasten to be reformed into the form of the new man, the more sincerely the later they do so. Let both these and those make progress, let them not fail nor grow weary, even if they do not yet fully feel in themselves that from which they too may say: 'Your name is oil poured out.' For the young maidens do not dare of themselves to address the bridegroom. Yet if they study to cling more closely to the footsteps of their teacher, they will at least be delighted by the odor of the oil that has been poured out, and will be stirred even by the perception of the odor to desire and to seek better things.
14.6: Often I myself, which I am not ashamed to confess, especially in the beginning of my conversion, hard and cold of heart, and seeking whom my soul might wish to love: for she could not yet love him whom she had not yet found, or certainly she loved him less than she wished, and on this account she was seeking that she might love more; whom she would by no means seek, unless she had already loved him in some measure. When, therefore, I was seeking him in whom my spirit, torpid and languid as it was, might grow warm again and rest; and no one came to help from any side, by whom, namely, the stiff winter which was binding the senses between us might be dissolved, and that springlike sweetness and spiritual pleasantness might return: then more and more my soul was languishing, and growing weary, and growing drowsy; sad from weariness and almost despairing, and muttering to herself that word: 'Before the face of this cold, who will endure?' (Ps. 147:17.) When suddenly, perhaps at the address, or even the look, of some spiritual and perfect man, and sometimes even at the mere memory of one dead or absent, the spirit was blowing, and the waters were flowing; and those tears were bread for me day and night. What is this, if not the odor of the anointing breathing out, with which that man had been steeped? For it was not the anointing, which, surely, was not reaching me except by means of a man. And on this account, although I was rejoicing in the gift, I was nevertheless confounded and humbled, because only a thin exhalation, and not a rich sprinkling, had come to me. Delighted, indeed, by the smell, not by the touch, I recognized that I was unworthy that God should grow sweet to me through himself. And now, if the same thing happens, I do indeed receive eagerly the gift that has been granted, and I hold it gratefully; but grieving, I grieve that I have not deserved it through myself, and that I have by no means received it, as the saying is, from hand to hand, though I was earnestly asking for this. I am ashamed, surely, to be moved by the memory of a man rather than by the memory of God. And then I cry out with a groan: 'When shall I come and appear before the face of God?' (Ps. 42:2.) I think that some of you also have experienced the same thing, and still experience it at times. In this matter, what is to be thought, if not that either our pride is convicted, or our humility is guarded, or brotherly charity is nourished, or desire is stirred up? One and the same food is medicine for the sick, and a diet for those apt to be sick: further, it both strengthens the weak and delights those who are well. One and the same food both heals languor and preserves health; and it nourishes the body, and has savor for the palate.
14.7: But let us return to the words of the bride, and let us take care to hear what she says in such a way that we also study to taste what she tastes. The bride, as I have said, is the Church. She is the one to whom more has been forgiven, and who loves more. What her rival casts at her as an insult, this she herself turns to her own advantage. Thence she is gentler unto correction, thence more patient unto labor; thence more ardent unto love, thence more sagacious unto caution; thence more humble for conscience, thence more acceptable for modesty; thence readier to obey, thence more devout and more solicitous unto thanksgiving. Finally, while that one, as has been said, is murmuring and calling to mind her own merits, and her labors, and the burden of the day and the heat, the Church recalls the benefit, saying: 'Your name is oil poured out.'
14.8: This, plainly, is the testimony of Israel unto the confessing of the name of the Lord; yet not Israel according to the flesh, but of him who is according to the spirit. For how should that one say this? Not that she does not have the oil, but she does not have it poured out. She has it, but stored away; she has it in books, but not in hearts. It clings outside, in the letter; she handles with her hands a vessel that is full, but also closed, nor does she open it that she may be anointed. Within, within is the anointing of the spirit; open and anoint, and you will no longer be a house that exasperates. What does the oil do in the vessels, if you do not feel it also in the members? What does it profit you to read over the loving name of the Savior in books, and not to have loving-kindness in your manners? It is oil; pour it out, and you will feel its power, which is threefold. But the Jew loathes these things; you, hear. I wish to say why the name of the bridegroom is compared to oil, which I had not yet said. And three causes of this thing occur. But because he is called by very many names, for the reason that none is found by which he may be properly spoken of (for he is ineffable), the Holy Spirit must first be called upon by us, that of the many he may deign to open to us through himself the one which he wishes to be understood in this place, since it did not please him to mark it in the writing. But this also at another time. For even if all things were now ready, and neither you were burdened nor I wearied, the hour nevertheless marks the end. Hold that to which I have made you attentive, so that there may be no need to repeat it tomorrow. This is what presses, this is what is in hand: to teach, namely, why the name of the bridegroom is compared to oil, and which of the names. And because I cannot say anything of myself, prayer is appointed, that the bridegroom himself may reveal it to us through his Spirit, Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom is honor and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

15.1: Kind is the Spirit of wisdom (Wis. 1:6), and he is not accustomed to be difficult to those who call upon him, who often, even before he is called upon, says: 'Behold, I am here' (Isa. 65:24). Hear now what, as you pray, he deigns to indicate through me concerning that which yesterday we put off for this very purpose, and receive the timely fruit of your prayers. Behold, I show the name which is deservedly compared to oil; and on what ground, I will say. You read, indeed, many titles of the Bridegroom scattered through the whole divine page, but I will gather them all for you into two. None, as I think, will you find which does not sound either the grace of piety or the power of majesty. The Spirit says so even through an instrument more familiar to himself: 'These two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, mercy' (Ps. 62:11, 12). Therefore according to majesty: 'Holy and terrible is his name' (Ps. 111:9); according to piety: 'There is no other name under heaven given to men, in which it is necessary that we be saved' (Acts 4:12). But it will become clearer by examples. 'This is,' he says, 'the name which they shall call him: the Lord, our just one' (Jer. 23:6). It is a name of power. Likewise: 'And his name shall be called Emmanuel' (Isa. 7:14); it suggests piety. Likewise he himself says of himself: 'You call me,' he says, 'Master and Lord' (John 13:13). The first is of grace, the second of majesty. For it is no less an act of piety to teach the mind knowledge than to provide food for the body. Again the prophet: 'His name shall be called,' he says, 'Wonderful, counselor, mighty God, father of the age to come, prince of peace' (Isa. 9:6). The first, the third, and the fourth sound majesty; the rest, piety. Which of these, then, is poured out? Surely the name of majesty and of power is in a certain way transfused into that which is of piety and of grace, and it itself is poured out abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior. The name, for example, which is God, does it not melt and fail into that which is God with us (Matt. 1:23), that is, into Emmanuel? So Wonderful, into that which is counselor; so God and mighty, into those which are father of the age to come and prince of peace; and the Lord our just one, into the merciful and compassionate Lord (Ps. 111:4). I am not saying anything new: once, no less, Abram was poured out into Abraham, and Sarai into Sarah (Gen. 17:5, 15); and we recall that even then the mystery of the saving outpouring was celebrated and prefigured.
15.2: Where now is that which among the ancients used to thunder forth as terribly as it did frequently: 'I am the Lord, I am the Lord?' (Exod. 20:2.) A prayer is dictated to me whose beginning, sweet with the paternal name, gives confidence of obtaining the petitions that follow. Servants are named friends (John 15:14, 15), and the resurrection is announced not merely to the disciples, but to the brothers (Matt. 28:10). Nor do I wonder if, when the fullness of time came, there was an outpouring of the name, God indeed fulfilling what he had promised through Joel, and pouring out of his Spirit upon all flesh (Joel 2:28); since I read that something of the sort happened long ago among the Hebrews also. I believe you are running on ahead, and already know what I wish to say. What sort of answer was it, I say, that was first given to Moses when he inquired: 'I am who I am?' and: 'He who is has sent me to you?' (Exod. 3:14.) I do not know whether even Moses himself would have grasped it so, if, of course, it had not been poured out. But it was poured, and it was grasped; and not only poured, but also poured out: for it had already been poured in. The heavens already had it, it had already been made known to the angels. But it was sent outside; and what had been so poured into the angels that it was also private to them, was poured out upon men as well, so that even then it might rightly have been cried from the earth: 'Your name is oil poured out' (Song 1:2): if the hateful obstinacy of an ungrateful people had not stood in the way. For he says: 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' (Exod. 3:6, 15).
15.3: Run, you nations; salvation is at hand, the name has been poured out, which whoever shall call upon, he will be saved. The God of angels names himself the God of men also. He sent oil into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel. Say to your brothers: 'Give us of your oil' (Matt. 25:8). If they will not, ask the Lord of the oil to send it to you also. Say: 'Take away our reproach' (Isa. 4:1). Let not, I ask, the ill-willed one insult your beloved, whom it pleased you to call from the ends of the earth, the more worthily, surely, the less worthy she was. Is it fitting, I beg, that a wicked servant should shut out those invited by a kindly householder? 'I am,' you say, 'the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' And no further? Pour out, pour out; open your hand still, and fill every living thing with blessing. Let them come from the east and the west, and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 8:11). Let them come, let the tribes come, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, unto the confessing of the name of the Lord (Ps. 122:4). Let them come and recline, let them feast and be delighted in gladness, and let one sound of one feasting resound everywhere in the voice of exultation and of confession (Ps. 42:4); 'Your name is oil poured out.' One thing I know: if we have Philip and Andrew as doorkeepers, we suffer no repulse at all, whoever of us seek the oil, whoever of us wish to see Jesus. Without delay Philip will tell Andrew; and Andrew and Philip will tell Jesus. But Jesus, what? Surely that which Jesus is. 'Unless the grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit' (John 12:24). Let the grain die, then, and let the harvest of the nations rise. It was necessary that Christ suffer, and rise from the dead, and that repentance and the remission of sins be preached in his name, not only in Judea, but also among all the nations; so that from the one name, which is Christ, thousands of thousands of believers may be called Christians, and may say: 'Your name is oil poured out.'
15.4: For I recognize the name which I read in Isaiah: 'He will call his servants,' he says, 'by another name, in which he who is blessed upon the earth shall be blessed in the Lord, amen' (Isa. 65:15, 16). O blessed name! O oil poured out on every side! How far? It runs from heaven into Judea, and from there into every land; and from the whole world the Church cries: 'Your name is oil poured out.' Poured out, plainly, in that it has not only flooded the heavens and the earth, but has also sprinkled the lower regions, so much so that at the name of Jesus every knee bends, of those in heaven, of those on earth, and of those under the earth, and every tongue confesses (Phil. 2:10, 11), and says: 'Your name is oil poured out.' Behold Christ, behold Jesus, each poured into the angels, each poured out upon men, and upon those men who had rotted like beasts in their own dung, God saving men and beasts, according as he has multiplied his mercy. How dear, how cheap! cheap, but wholesome. If it were not cheap, it would not be poured out for me; if it were not wholesome, it would not gain me. I am a sharer of the name, and I am also of the inheritance; I am a Christian; I am a brother of Christ. If I am what I am called, I am an heir of God, and a joint heir of Christ (Rom. 8:17). And what wonder if the name of the bridegroom has been poured out, when he himself also has been poured out? For he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7). Finally he says: 'I am poured out like water' (Ps. 22:14). The fullness of the Divinity has been poured out, dwelling upon earth bodily, so that from that fullness all of us who wear the body of death might take, and, filled with the life-giving odor, might say: 'Your name is oil poured out.' See what name has been poured out, and how, and how far. But why oil? For this I have not yet said. I had begun to say it in the previous sermon; but suddenly something else intervened which seemed to need to be preached. Although I broke off longer than I believed: which I think is nothing else than that the valiant woman, Wisdom, put her hand to the distaff, and her fingers grasped the spindle. For she knows how to draw a little wool or flax out into a long thread, and to extend it into the breadth of the web, and thus to clothe all her household in double garments (Prov. 31:19, 21). There is, without doubt, a likeness between the oil and the name of the bridegroom; nor did the Holy Spirit compare the one with the other idly. But I say it is in a certain threefold quality of the oil, that it gives light, feeds, and anoints, if you have nothing better. It fosters fire, nourishes flesh, soothes pain; light, food, medicine. See the same now also of the name of the bridegroom. Preached, it gives light; thought upon, it feeds; called upon, it soothes and anoints. And let us run through them one by one.
15.6: From where, do you think, comes so great and so sudden a light of faith in the whole world, if not from Jesus preached? Was it not in the light of this name that God has called us into his wonderful light, so that, enlightened, and seeing light in this light, Paul may rightly say: 'You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord?' (Eph. 5:8.) This name, finally, the same apostle was commanded to carry before kings, and nations, and the sons of Israel (Acts 9:15); and he was carrying the name as a light, and he was enlightening his country, and he was crying out everywhere: 'The night has gone before, but the day has drawn near.' 'Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armor of light: as in the day, let us walk honestly' (Rom. 13:12, 13). And he was showing to all the lamp upon the lampstand, announcing in every place Jesus, and him crucified. How this light shone in and dazzled the eyes of all who looked, when, going forth from the mouth of Peter like lightning, it made firm the bodily soles and feet of one lame man, and enlightened many who were spiritually blind! Did he not scatter fire, when he said: 'In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk?' (Acts 3:6.) Nor is the name of Jesus only light, but it is also food. Are you not strengthened as often as you remember it? What equally fattens the mind of one who thinks on it? what so repairs the senses that have been exercised, strengthens the virtues, quickens good and honorable manners, fosters chaste affections? Dry is all the food of the soul, if it is not steeped in this oil; tasteless it is, if it is not seasoned with this salt. If you write, it has no savor for me unless I read Jesus there. If you dispute or confer, it has no savor for me unless Jesus sounds there. Jesus is honey in the mouth, melody in the ear, jubilation in the heart. But it is also medicine. Is any of you sad? Let Jesus come into the heart, and from there leap into the mouth; and behold, at the rising of the light of the name, every cloud flees, and fair weather returns. Does someone slip into a crime, and run on, besides, to the snare of death by despairing? If he calls upon the name of life, will he not at once breathe again unto life? For whom has hardness of heart, as is usual, the torpor of sloth, bitterness of mind, the languor of weariness, ever stood before the face of the saving name? for whom has a spring of tears, perhaps dried up, not immediately burst forth more abundantly, and flowed more sweetly, when Jesus was called upon? For whom, panting and trembling in dangers, has the name of power, when called upon, not at once given confidence and driven off fear? For whom, I ask, tossing and wavering in doubts, has certainty not suddenly flashed out at the invocation of the bright name? For whom, distrusting in adversities and already on the point of failing, if the name of help has sounded, has strength been lacking? Surely these are the diseases and languors of the soul, and that is the medicine. Finally, it may also be proved: 'Call upon me,' he says, 'in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you shall honor me' (Ps. 50:15). Nothing so checks the assault of anger, calms the swelling of pride, heals the wound of envy, restrains the flux of luxury, extinguishes the flame of lust, tempers the thirst of avarice, and drives off the itch of every indecency. For when I name Jesus, I set before myself a man meek and humble of heart, kind, sober, chaste, merciful, and, finally, conspicuous for every honorableness and holiness, and that same one himself God almighty, who both heals me by his example and strengthens me by his help. All these things sound for me at once, when Jesus has sounded. I take, then, examples for myself from the man, and help from the mighty one; the former as the apothecary's spices, the latter as that with which I sharpen them: and I make a confection the like of which none of the physicians can make.
15.7: This electuary you have, O my soul, stored in the little vessel of this word, which is Jesus, surely health-giving, and such as is found ineffective against no pest of yours. Let it always be in your bosom, always in your hand, so that all your senses and acts may be directed unto Jesus. Finally, you are also invited: 'Set me,' he says, 'as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm' (Song 8:6). But this at another time. Now, however, you have that with which you may heal both the arm and the heart. You have, I say, in the name of Jesus, that with which you may either correct your acts when they are crooked, or complete them when they are less perfect; and likewise that with which you may either keep your senses, lest they be corrupted, or, if they are corrupted, heal them.
15.8: Judah also had certain men named Jesus, in whose empty names she glories. For those neither give light, nor feed, nor heal. Therefore the Synagogue is in darkness even until now, laboring with hunger and weakness; and she will not be healed nor filled, until she knows that my Jesus rules Jacob and the ends of the earth, and she turns at evening, and suffers hunger like the dogs, and goes about the city (Ps. 59:13, 6). And those, indeed, were sent on ahead, like the staff going before to the dead man of the prophet, and they could not interpret their own names; for they were empty. The staff was laid upon the dead man, and there was neither voice nor sense, because it was a staff. He descended who had sent the staff (2 Kgs. 4:29-35): and soon he saved his people from their sins, proving himself to be what was being said: 'Who is this, who even forgives sins' (Luke 7:49). Surely he who says: 'I am the salvation of the people' (Ps. 35:3). Now there is voice, now there is sense; and it is plain that he does not bear an empty name after the manner of the earlier ones. The salvation that has been poured in is felt, and the benefit is not kept silent. Within, sense; outside, voice. I am pricked, and I confess, and confession indicates life: for 'from the dead, as from one who is not, confession perishes' (Sir. 17:26). Behold life, behold sense. I have been raised perfectly; the resurrection is whole. Is the death of the body anything else than when it is deprived of sense and of life? Sin, which is the death of the soul, had left me neither the sense of compunction nor the voice of confession, and I was dead. He came who forgives sins, and he restored both, and he says to my soul: 'I am your salvation.' What wonder if death yields, where life has descended? Now it is believed with the heart unto justice, and confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). Now the boy yawns, and he yawns seven times (2 Kgs. 4:35), and he says: 'Seven times a day I have said praise to you' (Ps. 119:164), O Lord. See this number seven. It is a sacred number; it is not idle. But we keep this better for another sermon, in which, hungry and not disdainful, we may approach so good a feast, the bridegroom of the Church inviting us, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God over all, blessed unto ages. Amen.

16.1: What, then, does this number seven mean? For I do not know whether there is anyone among us so simple as to think these repetitions idle, and this number a matter of chance. Nor do I think that idle, either, that the prophet, lying upon the dead boy, contracted himself to the measure of the boy's body, joined his mouth to his mouth, and his eyes to his eyes, and his hands to his hands (2 Kgs. 4:34). The Holy Spirit caused all things to be done thus, and to be written thus, for the instruction, without doubt, of those spirits whom the treacherous company of a corrupt body besets, and whom the foolish wisdom of the world has taught to be foolish. For the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things (Wis. 9:15). Therefore let no one wonder, or take it ill, if in searching these things, as certain storehouses of the Holy Spirit, I am curious, since I know that thus one lives, and that in such things is the life of my spirit. I say, however, to those who, running ahead in wit, in every sermon demand the end almost before they have hold of the beginning, that I am a debtor to the slower also, and most of all; but neither is my study so much to explain words as to steep hearts. I must both draw and give to drink: which is not done by running through quickly, but by treating diligently, and by exhorting often. And yet, beyond my hope also, the discussion of the mysteries has held us long. I thought, I confess, that one sermon would suffice for this, and that we would quickly pass through this shady and hidden wood of allegories, and arrive at the plain of the moral senses by a journey of a single day, as it were: but it happened otherwise. For we have already spent two days on it, and the way still remains. The glance of the eye was flying from afar over the tops of the branches and the summits of the mountains; but the vastness of the valleys lying underneath, and the thickness of the thickets, was cheating the sight. Could I, for example, foresee the miracle of Elisha, that, while we were discussing the calling of the nations and the casting off of the Jews, it would thus leap suddenly into the midst? And now, since we have fallen upon it, let it not irk us to linger a little, afterward to return in due course to what we have broken off, since this is nonetheless food of souls. It happens also to dogs and hunters, often enough, to leave off from the beast they had set upon, and to follow another, which has perhaps come upon them unawares.
16.2: No small strength of confidence it gives me, that that great man, the prophet, mighty in work and in word, descending from the high mountain of the heavens, has deigned to visit me, though I am ashes and dust; to have mercy on the dead, to bend down to the one lying there, to contract himself and make himself equal to the little one, to share with the blind the light of his own eyes, and to loose the mute mouth with a kiss of his own mouth, and to strengthen the weak hands by the touch of his own. Sweetly I chew these things over, and my inward parts are filled, and my interior is fattened, and all my bones sprout praise. This he conferred once upon the whole company; this we feel to be carried out daily, each of us in ourselves, namely that light of understanding is given to the heart, and a word of edification to the mouth, and a work of justice to the hands. He gives one to feel faithfully, he gives one to bring forth usefully, he gives one to fulfill effectually. And there is a threefold cord, which is broken with difficulty, for drawing souls out of the prison of the devil, and drawing them after him to the heavenly kingdoms, if you feel rightly, if you speak worthily, if you confirm it by living. With his eyes he touched mine, adorning the forehead of the inward man with bright lights, faith and understanding. He joined his mouth to my mouth, and impressed the sign of peace upon the dead; because, while we were still sinners, he reconciled us to God, dead as we were to justice. He applied mouth to mouth, breathing again into my face the breath of life, but of a holier life than at first. For at first, indeed, he created me into a living soul; secondly, he reformed me into a life-giving spirit. He laid his hands upon mine, offering an example of good works, a form of obedience. Or, certainly, he put his hands to strong things, that he might teach my hands to battle, and my fingers to war.
16.3: And the boy yawned, he says, seven times (2 Kgs. 4:35). To have yawned once would have sufficed for the glory of displaying the miracle; but the multiplicity and the notable number warn of a mystery. If you attend to that huge body of the whole human race, at first indeed lifeless, you see the Church everywhere, from the time she received life with the prophet lying upon her, yawning as it were seven times; because she is accustomed to say praise seven times a day. If you turn to yourself, know that you live by the spiritual life in this, and fulfill this mystical number, if you subject the five of your sensuality to the two of charity, and present, according to the Apostle, your members to serve justice unto sanctification, which formerly you presented to serve iniquity unto iniquity (Rom. 6:19); or, certainly, if, bestowing that same five upon the salvation of your neighbors, you add these two to complete the seven, namely, to sing mercy and judgment to God.
16.4: I have also another seven yawnings, that is, seven experiences, without which the true and certain salvation of a spirit brought back to life does not stand at all: four belonging to the sense of compunction, three to the sound of confession. If you live, if there is voice, if there is sense, you too recognize the same things in yourself. Further, know that you have recovered sense in full, if you feel your conscience bitten by a fourfold compunction, by a double shame and a double fear: for, to complete the seven, a triple kind of confession attests the life, of which we shall see afterward. Does not holy Jeremiah also observe this number in his lament? You also, then, in your lamentation for yourself, having the prophetic form, think of God your maker, think also of your benefactor, think of your father, think of your Lord. You are guilty in regard to all; lament for each. To the first and the last let your fear answer, to the two middle ones, shame. A father, surely, is not feared, since he is a father. For it belongs to a father always to have mercy and to spare. And if he strikes, he strikes with a rod, not with a staff; and when he has struck, he heals. It is a father's voice: 'I will strike, and I will heal' (Deut. 32:39). There is, then, nothing for you to dread from a father, who, even if he sometimes strikes to amend, never does so to take vengeance. But for one who thinks that I have offended a father, there is certainly something to be ashamed of, even if nothing to be terrified by. Willingly he begot me by the word of truth; he did not shake me out by the goad of carnal desire, as the begetter of my flesh did. Then, too, he did not spare. The Only-begotten, for one so begotten. So he himself, indeed, showed himself a father to me, but I did not in turn show myself a son to him. With what face do I now lift my eyes to the countenance of so good a father, so bad a son? I am ashamed to have done things unworthy of my birth, I am ashamed to have lived degenerate from so great a father. Lead down streams of waters, my eyes; let confusion cover my face, let shame overflow my countenance, and let darkness take hold. Let my life fail in sorrow, and my years in groanings. Ah, the shame! what fruit did I have in the things of which I now blush? If I have sown in the flesh, from the flesh I shall reap nothing but corruption (Gal. 6:8); if in the world, it too passes away, and its concupiscence (1 John 2:17). What? perishable things, vain, and almost nothing, and things whose end is death, unhappy and mad, I was not ashamed to prefer to the love and honor of the eternal Father. I am confounded, I am confounded to hear: 'If I am a father, where is my honor?' (Mal. 1:6.)
16.5: But even if he were not a Father, he would overwhelm me with benefits. He raises up witnesses against me, to pass over other things without number: the food of this body, and the use of this time, and above all the blood of the beloved Son crying from the earth. I am ashamed of ingratitude, though, to the heap of confusion, I am accused also of having returned evils for goods, and hatred for love. There is, indeed, nothing at all to be feared by me from a benefactor, just as neither from a father. For he is a true benefactor, giving abundantly, and not reproaching (James 1:5). He does not reproach the gifts, because they are gifts; and he gave me his benefits, he did not sell them. Finally, his gifts are without repentance. But the more kindly I am forced to think of him, the more unworthily of myself. Blush, and grieve nonetheless, my soul; since, even if it befits him not to demand back and not to reproach, it altogether ill befits us to have been ungrateful and forgetful. Alas! what shall I even now at last return to the Lord for all that he has returned to me?
16.6: But if shame, perhaps slower, carries out its parts less fully, let fear indeed be stirred up to help. Let it be stirred, that it may stir. Set aside for a little the loving names of benefactor and of father, and turn to the sterner ones. For he who is read: 'Father of mercies, and God of all consolation' (2 Cor. 1:3); is read nonetheless: 'The Lord, God of vengeances' (Ps. 94:1); is read: 'God, a just and strong judge' (Ps. 7:11); is read: 'Terrible in counsels above the sons of men' (Ps. 66:5); is read: 'A jealous God' (Exod. 20:5). That he is a father, that he is a benefactor, is for you; that he is Lord and creator, is for himself; for he made all things for himself, as Scripture witnesses (Prov. 16:4). He, then, who defends and keeps for you what is yours: do you think he will not at some time be jealous also for himself? do you think he will not require the honor of his own sovereignty? For this the wicked man provoked God, because he said in his heart: 'He will not require it' (Ps. 10:13). And what is it to say in one's heart, 'He will not require it,' if not to have no fear that he will require it? But he will require it unto the last farthing: he will require it, and will repay abundantly those who act pride (Ps. 31:23). He will require service from the one he redeemed, honor and glory from the one he formed.
16.7: Suppose that the father dissembles, that the benefactor forgives; but the Lord and Creator will not; and he who spares the son will not spare what he has formed, will not spare a wicked servant: weigh of what dread and horror it is to have despised your maker and the maker of all, to have offended the Lord of majesty. It belongs to majesty to be feared, it belongs to a Lord to be feared, and most of all to this majesty, and to this Lord. For if it is sanctioned by human laws that one guilty of royal majesty, though a human majesty, be punished with the head; what will be the end of those who despise the divine omnipotence? He touches the mountains, and they smoke (Ps. 144:5); and does a vile little dust dare to provoke so tremendous a majesty, soon to be scattered by one light breath, and by no means to be gathered again? He, he is to be feared, who, after he has killed the body, has power to send also into hell (Luke 12:5). I dread hell, I dread the face of the judge, dreadful even to the angelic powers themselves. I tremble at the wrath of the mighty one, at the face of his fury, at the crash of a world falling, at the conflagration of the elements, at the mighty tempest, at the voice of the archangel, and at the harsh word. I tremble at the teeth of the infernal beast, at the belly of hell, at those roaring and prepared for food. I shudder at the gnawing worm, and the burning fire, the smoke, and the vapor, and the sulphur, and the spirit of storms; I shudder at the outer darkness. Who will give water to my head, and to my eyes a fountain of tears (Jer. 9:1), that with weepings I may come before the weeping, and the gnashing of teeth, and the hard bonds of hands and of feet, and the weight of chains pressing, constricting, burning, and not consuming? Woe is me, my mother! why did you bear me a son of sorrow, a son of bitterness, of indignation and of eternal weeping? Why taken up on the knees, why nursed at the breasts, born for the burning, and food of the fire?
16.8: He who is so affected has without doubt recovered sense, and in this double fear, and likewise in that shame equally double, he has four yawnings. He will add the three that remain from the voice of confession, and it will by no means now be said of him that there is neither voice nor sense, if, however, that confession has proceeded from a humble, simple, and faithful heart. Everything, then, that bites the conscience, confess humbly, purely, faithfully; and you have fulfilled these repetitions. There are those who glory when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things (Prov. 2:14); noting whom, the prophet says: 'They have proclaimed their sins as Sodom' (Isa. 3:9). But these I remove from this discussion, as men of the world: for what is it to us concerning those who are outside?
16.9: And yet, concerning those also who are religiously clothed, and have professed religion, we have sometimes heard some recall and boast most shamelessly of their past evils; which, for example, they once did, either bravely in a gladiator's fight, or cleverly in a contest of letters, or something else favorable indeed according to the vanity of the world, but according to the salvation of the soul harmful. pernicious, ruinous. This is the sign of a mind still worldly; and the humble habit which is worn by such men is not the merit of a holy newness, but a cover for the old decay. Some recall such things as if grieving and repenting; but, catching at glory by their intention, they do not wash away their offenses, but make sport of themselves: for God is not mocked (Gal. 6:7). They have not put off the old man, but cloak him with the new. The old leaven is not brought out or thrown away by that confession; but it is established, according to that word: 'My bones grew old, while I cried out all the day' (Ps. 32:3). I am ashamed to recall so great a forwardness in certain men, that they are not ashamed to boast, with a lamentable exultation, that even after taking the holy habit they have cunningly tripped someone up, and circumvented a brother in a matter of business; or that they have boldly returned a retaliation for an insult or a curse, that is, evil for evil; or a curse for a curse.
16.10: But there is a confession the more dangerously harmful the more subtly vain it is, when we do not fear to uncover even the dishonorable and the shameful things about ourselves, not because we are humble, but that we may be thought to be. But to seek praise from humility is not the virtue of humility, but its overthrow. The truly humble man wishes to be reputed vile, not to be proclaimed humble. He rejoices in contempt of himself. in this alone, surely, he is proud, that he despises praises. What is more perverse, or what more unworthy, than that confession, the guardian of humility, should serve pride, and that you should wish to seem better from that by which you are seen to be worse? A wonderful kind of boasting, that you cannot be thought holy unless you appear wicked. But such a confession, having the appearance of humility, not the virtue, not only does not deserve pardon, but even provokes wrath. Did it profit Saul, that he confessed himself to have sinned at the rebuke of Samuel? (1 Sam. 15:30.) Without doubt that confession was blameworthy, which did not wash away the fault. For when would the master of humility despise a humble confession, he to whom it is surely inborn to give grace to the humble? He could not at all have failed to be appeased, if the humility which sounded in the mouth had taken root in the heart. See why I said that confession ought to be humble.
16.11: But it ought also to be simple. Let it not please one to excuse the intention (perhaps because it lies hidden from men), if it is guilty; nor to lighten a fault which is grave; nor to shade it with another's persuasion, when no one has compelled the unwilling. That first thing is not a confession, but a defense; nor does it appease, but provokes. The next shows ingratitude; and the less the fault is reputed, the more the glory of the one who pardons is also diminished. For a benefit is given less willingly which is felt to come less gratefully or less necessarily. He therefore judges pardon away from himself, who lessens the gift of the giver: which, indeed, everyone does who tries to lighten his guilt with words. Finally, let the example of the first man dissuade you, who indeed did not deny the fault, and yet did not obtain pardon, without doubt on account of the mixing in of the woman's guilt (Gen. 3:12). It is a kind of excuse, when you are accused, to accuse another. Further, how wishing to excuse yourself when you are rebuked is not only not at all fruitful, but even ruinous, ask holy David. For he calls the words of malice excuses in sins, praying and beseeching that his heart not turn aside into them (Ps. 141:4). Rightly, indeed. For he sins against his own soul who excuses himself, thereby driving from himself the medicine of indulgence, and so shutting off life from himself with his own mouth. And what greater malice is there than to be armed against one's own salvation, and to pierce yourself with the point of your own tongue? Finally, he who is wicked to himself, to whom is he good? (Sir. 14:5.)
16.12: But let the confession also be faithful, so that you confess in hope, distrusting the pardon not at all, lest with your own mouth you not so much justify yourself as condemn yourself. Judas, certainly, the betrayer of the Lord, and Cain the fratricide, confessed, and distrusted: the one said, 'I have sinned, betraying innocent blood' (Matt. 27:4); the other, 'My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon' (Gen. 4:13); and though true, the unfaithful confession profited them nothing. These three observances of confession, then, joined to the four of compunction above, fulfill the number seven.
16.13: Now, indeed, thus pricked, and thus confessed, and therefore certain of life from your own experience, you are also certain, as I think, that he is by no means called Jesus by an empty name, he who was able and willed to work such things in you, and that the staff which he had sent ahead did not follow emptily. He did not come emptily, because he did not come empty. For how empty, he in whom fullness dwelt? Nor was the spirit given to him by measure. Finally, he also came in the fullness of time (Gal. 4:4), thereby indicating that he came full. Well full, he whom the Father anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows (Ps. 45:7); he anointed and sent him full of grace and truth (John 1:14). He anointed, that he might anoint. All have been anointed by him who have deserved to receive of his fullness. Therefore he says: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to announce to the meek, that I might heal the contrite of heart, that I might preach pardon to the captives, and opening to those who are shut up, that I might preach the acceptable year of the Lord' (Isa. 61:1, 2). He was coming, as you hear, to anoint our contritions, and to soothe the pains; and therefore he came anointed, he came gentle and meek, and of great mercy to all who call upon him. He knew that he was descending to the sick, and he showed himself such as he ought. And because the infirmities were many, the provident physician took care to bring many medicines also. He brought the spirit of wisdom and of understanding, the spirit of counsel and of fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and of piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord.
16.14: Do you see how many vials full of perfumes the heavenly physician prepared for healing the wounds of that wretch who fell among thieves? They are seven in number, fitted, perhaps, to stir up the seven yawnings mentioned before. For the spirit of life was in the vials. From these, surely, he poured oil into my wounds; he poured wine also, but less than of the oil. For so it suited my infirmities, that he should exalt mercy above judgment, just as oil poured in is carried above the wine. He brought, then, five jars of oil, and of wine only two. For the wine was fear alone, and fortitude; the remaining five, by their proper sweetness, signify oil. Finally, in the spirit of fortitude, like a mighty man grown merry with wine (Ps. 78:65), he descended to the lower regions, he shattered the gates of brass, and broke the bars of iron; he bound the strong one, and snatched away the vessels of captivity. He descended nonetheless in the spirit of fear, but as one to be feared, not as one afraid.
16.15: O Wisdom! with how great an art of healing do you restore health to my soul in wine and in oil, mightily sweet, and sweetly mighty! mighty for me, and sweet to me. Finally, you reach from end to end mightily, and you dispose all things sweetly, driving off the enemy, and cherishing the weak. Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; I will sing psalms and confess your name, and I will say: 'Your name is oil poured out' (Song 1:2). Not wine poured out (for I do not wish you to enter into judgment with your servant), but oil, because you crown me in mercy and in compassions (Ps. 103:4). Oil, plainly, which, while it floats above all the liquids with which it is mixed, clearly designates that name which is above every name. O name most sweet and most pleasant! o name most bright, most choice, and most lofty, and exalted above all unto ages! This is truly the oil which cheers the face of a man, which fattens the head of one who fasts, so that he does not feel the oil of the sinner. This is the new name, which the mouth of the Lord has named (Isa. 62:2). Which was also called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb (Luke 2:21). This, not the Jew only, but whoever shall call upon it, will be saved (Joel 2:32); so far has it been poured out on every side. This the Father gave to the Son, the bridegroom of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God over all, blessed unto ages. Amen.

17.1: Do we think that enough progress has been made in the sanctuary of God, while we search out the wonderful sacrament; or do we still dare, if anything remains, to follow the Spirit to the inner places, to search further? For this Spirit searches not only the hearts and reins of men, but also the deep things of God: and whether to our own things, or to the high things, I follow him securely wherever he goes. Only let him guard our hearts and our understandings, lest perhaps, when he is not present, we think him present, and, going astray, follow our own sense in his place. For he comes, and goes as he wills; and no one easily knows whence he comes, or where he goes (John 3:8). But this, perhaps, one may not know without loss of salvation: for the rest, when he comes, or when he goes, that is ignored most dangerously indeed. For when these dispensatory changes of the Holy Spirit around us are not observed most watchfully, it comes about that you neither desire him absent, nor glorify him present. For he who on this account withdraws, that he may be sought more eagerly: in what way is he sought, if it is not known that he is absent? And again, he who graciously returns for this, that he may console: how is he received worthily according to his majesty, if it is not even felt that he is present? The mind, then, which does not know the departure, lies open to seduction; and that which does not observe the return will be ungrateful for the visitation.
17.2: Elisha once asked something of his master, when he perceived that his departure was near; nor did he obtain it, as you know, except indeed on this condition, if he should see when he was taken from him (2 Kgs. 2:9, 10). This happened to them in a figure, but it has been written for our sake. We are taught and warned by the prophetic example to be watchful and solicitous about the work of our salvation (which, with a wonderful subtlety and sweetness of his divine art, the Spirit unceasingly carries on in the inmost part of us). Never, surely, without our consciousness, let the anointing which teaches of all things be taken from us, if we wish not to be defrauded of the doubled gift. Never, when he has come, let him find us unprepared, but always with faces lifted up, and with bosoms opened wide to the large blessing of the Lord. What sort of men, finally, does he seek? Men like those waiting for their lord, when he returns from the wedding (Luke 12:36): who, surely, never returns from those abundant delights of the heavenly table with an empty hand. One must watch, then, and watch at every hour, because we do not know at what hour the Spirit will come, or again will go away. The Spirit goes and returns; and he who stands while he holds him must needs fall when he deserts him; but he is not dashed down, because the Lord again puts his hand beneath. And he does not cease to alternate these changes in those who are spiritual, or rather in those whom he himself therefore intends to make spiritual, visiting at dawn, and suddenly proving. Finally, the just man falls seven times, and seven times rises again (Prov. 24:16): if, however, he falls in the day, so that he sees himself fall, and knows that he has fallen, and desires to rise again, and seeks the hand of one who helps, and says: 'O Lord, in your will you have granted strength to my beauty; you have turned your face from me, and I have been troubled' (Ps. 30:7).
17.3: It is one thing to doubt about the truth, which you must needs suffer when the Spirit does not breathe at all; and another to savor falsehood, which you easily avoid, if you are not ignorant of that ignorance of yours, so that you too may say: 'And if I have been ignorant of anything, my ignorance is with me' (Job 19:4). It is the sentence of holy Job; recognize it. Of ignorance, a most evil mother, there are likewise two most evil daughters, falsity and doubtfulness: the former more wretched, the latter more pitiable; the former more ruinous, the latter more troublesome. When the Spirit speaks, each yields: and there is not only truth, but certain truth. For that Spirit is of truth, to which falsity is contrary; and he is also of wisdom, which, since it is the brightness of eternal life, and reaches everywhere on account of its purity, does not admit the obscurity of the ambiguous. To be guarded against, surely, when this Spirit does not speak, even if not the troublesome doubtfulness, certainly the detestable falsity. For it is one thing, under uncertainty, to think this or that by way of opinion, and another rashly to affirm what you do not know. Either, then, let the Spirit always speak, which is by no means in our power; or, when it pleases him to be silent, let him indicate this itself, and at least speak his own silence, lest, thinking that he goes before us falsely, we, badly secure, follow our own error in his place; and if he has held us in suspense with the ambiguous, let him not abandon us to a lie. There is one who utters a falsehood doubtfully, and does not lie; and there is one who affirms a truth which he does not know, and does lie. For the former does not say that what is not, is; but he says that he believes what he believes, and he says what is true, even if this is not true which he believes; and the latter, when he says that he is certain of that of which he is not certain, does not say what is true, even if what he asserts is true.
17.4: With these things premised for the caution of such as are inexperienced, I will now follow the Spirit, as I trust, going before, yet with the same caution, if I can, which I premised; and I will try myself to do what I teach, lest it be said to me also: 'You who teach others, do you not teach yourself' (Rom. 2:21), a distinction surely to be made between things manifest and things doubtful, and those, of course, not to be brought into doubt, nor these rashly to be affirmed. Which very thing is to be hoped for from the teaching of the Spirit: for our own industry does not at all suffice for it. Who of men knows whether that which the previous sermon (from which, namely, if I remember well, this is the fourth) laid open as judged by God among men, had also already gone before as a judgment made in the realms above.
17.5: What I say is this. Do you think that Lucifer, who rose in the morning, but was lifted up too soon, before he was turned into darkness, himself also envied the human race the infusion of the oil, so that already then, indignant, he muttered by himself, saying within himself in a certain way: 'Why this waste?' This I do not assert that the Spirit says, but neither do I say that he contradicts it; for I do not know. But it could have happened, if, however, it not be thought incredible, that one full of wisdom and perfect in beauty could have foreknown that men would be, and even that they would advance to an equal glory. But if he foreknew, he saw it without doubt in the Word of God, and he envied it in his spite, and he set himself to have them as subjects, disdaining them as companions. 'They are weaker,' he says, 'and lower by nature; it is not fitting that they be fellow citizens, nor equals in glory.' Or does that presumed ascent, and that session signifying a mastership, perhaps betray this impious plot of his: 'I will ascend,' he says, 'above the high mountain, and I will sit on the sides of the north' (Isa. 14:13), whereby he would then obtain the likeness of the Most High, if, just as he, sitting above the cherubim, governs every angelic creature, so he too should sit on high, and rule the human race? Far be it! He meditated iniquity in his bed; let iniquity lie to itself. We acknowledge no other judge than the author. Not the devil, but the Lord will judge the world of the earth, and he himself is our God unto age of age; he himself will rule us unto ages.
17.6: In heaven, then, he conceived sorrow, and in paradise he brought forth iniquity, the offspring of malice, the mother of death and of miseries; and the first parent of all, pride. For although by the envy of the devil death entered into the world (Wis. 2:24), yet the beginning of every sin is pride (Sir. 10:15). But what did it profit him? Nonetheless you are in us, O Lord, and your name has been invoked upon us; and the people of acquisition says it, the Church of the redeemed says it: 'Your name is oil poured out.' When I am cast out, you pour it out after me, and into me; because, when you have been angry, you will remember mercy. Yet Satan received a kingdom over all the sons of pride, made the prince of this darkness, so that pride also might serve the kingdom of humility, while in that one temporal principality of his, and such as it is, he establishes many humble, high, and eternal kings. A pleasant judgment, that that proud one, the hammerer of the humble, unknowing, forges everlasting crowns for those same ones, by attacking all, and by succumbing to all. For everywhere and always the Lord will judge the peoples, and will save the sons of the poor, and will humble the false accuser. Everywhere, and always, he will defend his own, he will drive off those who harm, and he will take the rod of sinners away from above the lot of the just, so that the just may not stretch out their hands to iniquity (Ps. 125:3); and there will be a time at last when he will altogether break the bow, and shatter the arms, and burn the shields with fire. You, wretch, set a seat for yourself in the north, a region cloudy and cold; and behold, the needy are raised from the dust, and the poor from the dung, that they may sit with princes, and hold the throne of glory, and you may grieve that this is fulfilled: 'The poor and the needy shall praise your name' (Ps. 74:21).
17.7: Thanks to you, father of orphans and judge of wards: the curdled mountain has grown warm upon us, the fat mountain, the heavens have dropped at the face of the God of Sinai, the oil has been poured out, the name has been enlarged, which the wicked one envied us, and us to it; enlarged, I say, even to the hearts and mouths of little ones, and in the mouth of infants and of nursing children praise is perfected. But the sinner will see and be angry; and as the wrath is implacable, so the flame is inextinguishable, which is already prepared for him and for his angels. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this. How do you love me, my God, my love? how do you love me, remembering me everywhere, everywhere jealous for the salvation of the needy and the poor, not only against proud men, but also against the sublime angels? In heaven and on earth you judge, O Lord, those who harm me, you fight down those who attack me; everywhere you come to help, everywhere you stand by, everywhere you are at my right hand, O Lord, lest I be moved. These things I will sing to the Lord in my life, I will sing psalms to my God as long as I am. These are his virtues, these the wonders which he has done. This is the first and greatest judgment, which the virgin Mary, knowing the secrets, opened to me: 'He has put down,' she says, 'the mighty from their seat, and exalted the humble.' 'The hungry he has filled with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty' (Luke 1:52, 53). But the second is like this, which you have already heard, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind (John 9:39). In these two judgments let the poor man console himself, and say: 'I have remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord, and I have been comforted' (Ps. 119:52).
17.8: But let us return to ourselves, and let us search out our ways; and that we may be able to do this in truth, let us call upon the Spirit of truth, and call him back from the height to which he had led us, so that he may go before us even to ourselves, since without him we can do nothing. Nor is it to be feared that he disdains to come down to us, who rather is indignant if we attempt even a very little without him. For he is not one who goes and does not return, but he leads us and leads us back from glory to glory, as the Spirit of the Lord, sometimes catching us up to himself in his light, sometimes tempering himself, and enlightening our darkness, so that whether above us or with us, we may always walk in the light, always as sons of light. We have passed through the shadows of the allegories; we have come to searching out the moral senses. Faith has been built up, let life be instructed; the understanding has been exercised, let action be prescribed. For a good understanding is for all who do it (Ps. 111:10), if, however, both action and understanding are directed to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God over all, blessed unto ages. Amen.
